notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1173.tmp1173.opp-lat: The edition's text is disordered here. In the second line filed under ref .3, the quotation from Gregory Nazianzen breaks off after 'quo requiesfuit ab oporibus : tur.' The text then repeats, word for word, the long passage on souls punished in bodies from 'Si vero, juxta Origenis blasphemiam' to 'fabulas dicere'. Both copies are translated as given, and '[...]' marks the break. 'tur.' appears to be the stray end of a lost word. The repeated passage continues in the 'after' text, so the duplication looks like a fault in the scan or the edition. The text twice cites '1 Cor. v'; the verse quoted is 2 Cor. 5:10. 'Petri archon' is a misreading of Peri Archon (On First Principles). 'Zach. xn' is Zech. 12:1. 'John, holy patriarch of Constantinople' is John Chrysostom; the text says 'eleventh homily' but the reference reads Homil. XIII. The oration 'on the New Sunday' is cited as Orat. 43; it is usually numbered Oration 44.

Line 1: 'Mic nalos' is read as 'sic natos' and 'regem judici' as 'regem induci'. 'quid sit offendere' is taken as 'what it is to stumble (i.e. sin)'. The Gregory oration cited 'in novam dominicam' is given as Orat. 43 in the edition; the New Sunday oration is usually numbered 44.

The Lazarus parable is cited as Luke 19 in the text; it is Luke 16. In Gregory's quotation 'studiosum' likely renders Greek mystes ('initiate'), translated accordingly. Athanasius' 'de mente animam esse definientes' read as 'demente' split in the scan.

13: 'in illud' read for 'in iliad'. 13: 'Docet enim nos, in principio fuisse humanam rationem' seems elliptical or corrupt; Basil denies that human reason was in the beginning, so '[that some suppose]' is supplied for sense. 14: 'Cur ac proditor' read as 'fur ac proditor' (thief and traitor). 14: 'devictas' probably for 'devinctas' (bound). 17: the Pauline citation is 2 Cor. 5:10, though the edition gives 1 Cor. 15. 18: 'Fingetis' read as 'Fingens'. 18: the closing quotation mark, absent in the edition, is supplied before the final sentence, which is Justinian's own conclusion.

Line 19: 'aquam esse cogitemus *' is defective; Basil's Greek has 'let us think of water as water', which is translated. Justinian then quotes Basil as 'Sermo quidam nobis est ad eos qui sunt ab Ecclesia', which differs from the wording 'ad eos qui ab Ecclesia exciderunt' given just before; both are translated as they stand. Line 20: the citation 'John 20' for 'firstfruits of those who sleep' is the edition's (the phrase is from 1 Cor. 15); 'Eccl. II' is Sirach 2. Line 23: 'quam quantus est terror' is awkward and probably corrupt; rendered by the sense of Gregory's Greek ('more just than terrible'). Line 25: 'Dan. xvn' read as Dan. 7; '11 Thess. i' as 2 Thess. 1.

Line 28: the Latin is garbled ('a esse enim est minus: quod verum Patrem Filius'); read as 'esse enim est [he is being]; minor vero Patre Filius', with 'a' taken as a footnote mark. Line 42: 'judicium diurnum' read as 'divinum'. Biblical references are given as printed though wrong: 'Jer. VI' is Isaiah 6, 'Prov. XLIV' is Psalm 44 (45), 'Prov. IX' should be Prov. 8, '1 Cor. v' likely 1 Cor. 1. Line 41: trailing 'a' treated as a footnote mark. Line 43 is obscure in the Latin and translated literally.

Line 53: 'dolis' read as 'solis' (soul of the sun); line 54: 'bol' read as 'Sol'; line 55: 'leri' read as 'fieri'. Line 63: 'materiales' sits oddly beside the bracketed '[ratione praeditas]'; the Greek anathema has 'animate and rational', so 'materiales' may be a corruption. Line 68: 'iidem eoascuntur' is corrupt; rendered as '[faith] ... are found', on a likely reading such as 'fidem noscuntur'. Line 69: the Plato quotation ('educitur ct aLit') read as 'educitur et abit'.

In the titulature 'Anticu.' is read as Anticus. 'unicus carnii' in the long final passage is evidently 'unitus carni' (united to flesh), parallel to 'uniti spiritui'. 'unitas [unitionem]' and similar bracketed alternatives are the edition's; 'union' is used throughout. In 'supra rationem [orationem]' the alternative would give 'beyond speech'.

This stretch belongs to Justinian's confession of the right faith (the edict of c. 551), not to the treatise against Origen named in 'about'. Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'verhi', 'Chrislus', 'Dens', 'sceun . dum', 'saLona' for 'natura', 'Nani' for 'Nam'). 'Successa/Successus' is Succensus, bishop of Diocaesarea, recipient of Cyril's letters. Bracketed variants such as '[substitit]', '[ratione sola]', '[et Spiritui Græc.]' and '[mysterio Christi Græc.]' are the edition's readings from the Greek, kept in brackets. 'In quibus' in 79 follows the edition's '[de]' correction ('of whom').

Line 85: 'occasionem sui erroris faciunt' is read as making the number of natures the pretext of their error. Line 86: 'Magnum Apollinaristam' is rendered as 'Magnus the Apollinarist'; it may be corrupt, since the Council of 381 condemned Apollinarius himself. 'mathema' is rendered 'lesson' (Greek mathēma, a taught formula). 'Eunonium' is read as Eunomius, and 'Successum' as Succensus. The Scripture references are kept as printed, apart from obvious scanning slips.

The edition's numbering skips ref 96. In anathema 6, 'nos' is read as 'non'. In 12, 'in Manete Chalcedonensi concilio' is read as 'in sancto Chalcedonensi concilio' and 'rectam ademi confieri' as 'rectam fidem confiteri'. In 11, the edition's bracketed note '[Hic autem etiam Gr.]' records a variant from the Greek and is rendered simply as 'also'. In 13, 'quam sine inquisitione... ab ipsa Nestorio condemnato' lacks a governing verb; 'saying' is supplied. Also in 13, '[secundum unam]' is an editorial insertion and its sense is unclear. The anathema clause in 13 appears mid-passage, before the long argument about the letter.

Line 105: the clause on the Church of Mopsuestia ("propter blasphemias, ob quas paganis cum invenisset quod paganis et Judaeis et Sodomitanis...") is garbled in the printed text; the translation gives the evident sense. In the same line, "quibus si tradere noluerint ... ttedant" is read as "credere ... credant", and "nec viri haeretici" as "nec vivi haeretici". "cot. I" is taken as Acts 1.

Line 106: 'ani autem' read as 'alii autem'. The attribution of the posthumous anathemas to Damasus alongside the synod of Sardica (343) is chronologically odd (Julius was pope then); the text is translated as it stands. Line 107: 'Eo... tychen' read as Eutychen; '1 Cor. vII' corrected to 1 Cor. 1 (the cross as foolishness); 'Bosphorii' read as Bosporius, bishop of Colonia. 'Sozomenus... et Theodoretus, qui multas...' — the relative clause apparently refers to Theodoret only. Line 109: 'Augusto' read as Augustinus; the quotation from Augustine shifts into the first person in the Latin and is rendered so. Reference numbering skips 108 in the edition.

The heading reads 'Theodosio Mopsuesteno', evidently an error for 'Theodoro'; translated as Theodore. In Cyril's letter the references printed as 'Isa. XVII', 'Joan. I' and '1 Cor. ix' are corrected to Isa. 7 and John 3 (the latter two quotations are John 3:13 and Eph. 5:31 / Gen. 2:24, cited as 'the Apostle'); the reference after the Ephesians quotation is omitted as wrong. 'de eo sectatoribus ejus' seems to lack 'et'; supplied. 'priori concilio' read as 'prius' per the editor's note.

The line opens mid-sentence ('patres'), the preceding words being absent from the text as held. The heading in the preceding stretch reads 'Theodosio Mopsuesteno', evidently for Theodoro. 'Ac primam sanctam Ephesinam synodum' is taken as a further object of 'contra'. 'Concepisti' is read as concepistis (scanning error). The biblical reference is Isaiah 50:11.

nodes.text: THE BOOK OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN AGAINST ORIGEN
Treatise of the most pious emperor Justinian, sent to Menas, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of the fortunate city and patriarch, against the impious Origen and his abominable opinions.

It has always been our concern, and still is now, that the correct and irreproachable faith of Christians, and the condition of the most holy catholic and apostolic Church of God, should be kept free of disturbance in every respect. This is our first and oldest care: through it, we have believed, the empire was handed down to us by God in the present age and is preserved, and the enemies of our state are subdued; and in the age to come we hope to obtain mercy in the sight of his goodness. For even if the enemy of the human race devises various occasions by which he strives to harm the souls of men, yet the loving-kindness of God, breaking and emptying his wickedness and malice and refuting his adversaries, does not allow his flock to suffer loss or to be scattered. We have said this because it has been reported to us that some who do not have the fear of God in their minds, and do not hold to the distinction of right doctrine by which whoever knows the truth is saved, have abandoned the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers whom the catholic Church of God has as teachers, through whom every heresy everywhere has been driven out and the orthodox faith declared, and are asserting Origen and his dogmas, which are akin to the errors of the pagans, the Arians and the Manichaeans, and through which he fell into the pit. How can such people be counted among Christians, when they defend a man who strove to hand on what the pagans, Manichaeans, Arians and other heretics hold? Above all, he dared to utter blasphemies against the holy and consubstantial Trinity itself: that the Father is greater than the Son, the Son than the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit than the other spirits. Furthermore he added this to his impiety, saying that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son; that the Son himself and the Holy Spirit are creatures; and that what we are to the Son, the Son is to the Father. To his blasphemies he also joined this, in the first book of the Peri Archon, saying in these words: "In that beginning which is grasped by the mind, God by his will established as great a number of intelligible substances as could suffice; for it must be said that the power of God is finite, and its limitation is not to be removed under the pretext of praise and fine words; for if the divine power were infinite, it would necessarily not even understand itself, since by nature the infinite cannot be comprehended. He therefore made as many as he could grasp and hold under his providence; just as he also prepared as much matter as he could govern, arrange and adorn." Could Origen have uttered any greater blasphemy against God? He devises grades in the holy Trinity, wishing thereby to introduce a multitude of gods, and monstrously asserts that the very power of God is limited. And it belongs to his fabulous invention, a thing full of every impiety, to say that all genera and species are coeternal with God; and that rational beings which sinned, and therefore fell from their state, were cast into bodies by way of punishment in proportion to their sins, and, when purged, are raised again to their original state, having laid aside all wickedness and bodies; and again a second and a third time, and many times, are cast into different bodies for punishment. Further, he holds that different worlds have existed and exist, both past and future. Who is so foolish that on hearing these things he does not shudder in his mind at their extreme impiety? Who would not curse the insane Origen, who invented such blasphemies against God and committed them to writing? These, as being forbidden to all Christians and bearing manifest proofs of impiety, we have judged it superfluous to dignify with refutation. Therefore, if all heretics, perhaps for the perversity of one or two dogmas, have been cast out of the most holy Church and subjected to anathema with their dogmas, which Christian at all will endure defending Origen and his depraved writings, who uttered so many blasphemies and furnished almost all heretics with so much material for destruction and blasphemy, and was therefore long ago subjected to anathema by the holy Fathers together with his wicked dogmas? For even if one grants that Origen, though fighting against God, expressed something of right doctrine in his wicked writings (which is also found among other heretics), that is not his own but belongs to the holy Church of God; and he contrived this very thing maliciously to deceive the simpler. For, nourished on the fictions of the pagans and intending to spread them, he pretended to interpret the divine Scriptures, so that by maliciously mixing his abominable doctrine with the records of sacred letters in this way he might introduce his pagan and Manichaean error and Arian madness, and might lure those who had not accurately understood sacred Scripture. For what else did Origen expound but the doctrine of Plato, who had spread the madness of the pagans? Or from whom else did Arius borrow to compound his own poisons? He, to the destruction of his own soul, devised grades in the holy and consubstantial Trinity. And is he far from the Manichaean, when he says that the souls of men are sent into bodies for punishment because of sins? He asserts that they were at first minds and holy powers, then grew sated with divine contemplation and, turned to the worse, thereby grew cold from the love of God, and hence were called by the Greek name ψυχαί [souls], and were put into bodies by way of punishment. This alone would have sufficed for his complete condemnation, since it arose from the impiety of the pagans. For since God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness (Gen. 1), it follows from his empty talk that the body alone, without the soul, was made in the image and likeness of God, if the soul pre-existed at all and, once the body was made, was cast into it, or sent into it as into a vessel. And it will be altogether necessary to say that God himself, the maker of man, is a body, since he made a body in his own image and likeness. But how can a body be the image of the incorporeal? Therefore far be it that Christians should assent to these things. If, however, according to Origen's blasphemy, souls pre-existed and were sent down into bodies as punishment for their sins, so that being corrected they might come to their senses, they ought to sin no more. For if the body was given to the soul as a punishment for sins, so that it might be corrected by pains to honour God, how does the body help and strengthen it to sin, which does not happen to those who are punished? For chains, prisons, fetters and, to put it briefly, all such things restrain the iniquities and sins of those who are already paying the penalty. Nor are chains put on one who has sinned to help him sin more, but so that by the torment of the chains he may cease from sinning. Hence it is plain that souls were not sent into bodies to chastise earlier sins, as those people prattle, but that God fashioned body and soul together, that is, the complete man. Therefore we await a recompense for the things done by us through the body, whether good or evil; for this is what the divine apostle Paul also teaches us, saying: For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things [done] through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (1 Cor. 5). The apostle's words must therefore be attended to: for he did not say that the one judged must receive according to what he did before the body. But if a man is either punished or deservedly rewarded by him who judges the earth only for the things he did through the body, and no mention is made of sins committed before, it is plain that souls do not exist before bodies. For if they pre-existed, the Apostle would have said: things done both through the body and before the body. That the souls of men use intelligence and reason is admitted; we think not even those who defend Origen deny this. Let those who agree with Origen tell us, then: their souls (if indeed, as they assert, they existed before bodies), before they entered them, in what rank were they, or what were they doing? For if they existed before, they ought to know where they were, or how they came here; but if they can in no way say this (for it is not true), it is clear that they are telling fables. But perhaps they may say that souls, after they have entered bodies, are then able to discern and know what they do. If they say this, it follows from their empty argument that the body has more worth and honour than the soul, since it gives it intelligence and reason as a benefit; yet to assert this is full of madness and absurdity. And why, if the soul existed before the body, as they say, does it need instruction after it has come into the body, and is gradually trained and advances to better and more perfect things? For if it existed before, it would certainly know what is useful and would need no teaching, nor, as one already possessed of knowledge, be educated with care and diligence; and if it knew what it is to offend, it would not be taught what it had known before. But if it is taught, as one in ignorance, it did not know before; if it did not know before, it did not exist before. And it is evident that it did not exist before. For God alone is the cause of our coming into being; who, as he made us when we were not, so guards and saves us once born by his grace and his own hand, if we are shown to be worthy and fit. For God, who said: Let us make man in our image and likeness (Gen. 1), made both at once, that is, he formed the body and created the intelligent and rational soul. For he at once fashioned the body and established the soul, presenting the complete man; for man is neither a body without a soul nor a soul without a body. But if the soul pre-existed, as Origen raves, for what reason did the most holy prophet Zechariah say: Forming the spirit of man within him (Zech. 12)? For if it existed before, he ought rather to have said, 'pouring in as into a vessel', or 'sending down the spirit of man into him'. But when the prophet says 'forming', he shows that God by his own power and goodness made the soul, like the body, from things not pre-existing. Since, then, man, as has been said, was made in the image and likeness of God and was deemed worthy of the divine breath, it is plain from this that the soul was created not only intelligent and rational but also immortal, so that it might rule over all things made on earth. For this is what was said of the soul by Gregory the Theologian: that it is from God, and divine, and shares in heavenly nobility; not, as some suppose and say, that the soul is of the divine substance, but that it was made by the breath of God and received grace from him to be intelligent, rational and immortal, and not to die together with the body like the irrational animals, but by grace to share in heavenly nobility, that is, immortality. To this John, holy patriarch of Constantinople, bears witness in the eleventh homily on the creation; for he says (Homil. 13 on Gen. 2): "And he breathed, it says, into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Here some unskilled men, moved by their own thoughts and having nothing befitting God in mind, nor considering the condescension of the words, dare to say that the soul is from the substance of God. O insanity, O madness!" So much, then, the Father on the matter in hand. Consider, moreover, that of all the other things made on earth God said: let there be, and let the earth bring forth, and it was done (ibid.); but of man he says: Let us make man; and not only 'let us make', but 'in our image and likeness'; and taking dust from the earth he formed man with his own hands, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. From this, then, it can be seen how God made man more honourable and precious than all the other creatures on earth: all the others he made by a word: he spoke, and they were made; but man, as has been said, he made with his own hands, according to divine Scripture; and whatever he had made on earth he subjected to man, who was made on the sixth day, so that, all earthly creatures having been already made and prepared for him, he might rule over them, himself obeying the command of his maker. This too the holy Gregory the Theologian teaches us in his oration on the New Sunday (Orat. 43); for he says: "Thus something is counted first among the days, and second, and third, and so on up to the seventh day, on which there was rest from works: [...] If, however, according to Origen's blasphemy, souls pre-existed and were sent down into bodies as punishment for their sins, so that being corrected they might come to their senses, they ought to sin no more. For if the body was given to the soul as a punishment for sins, so that it might be corrected by pains to honour God, how does the body help and strengthen it to sin, which does not happen to those who are punished? For chains, prisons, fetters and, to put it briefly, all such things restrain the iniquities and sins of those who are already paying the penalty. Nor are chains put on one who has sinned to help him sin more, but so that by the torment of the chains he may cease from sinning. Hence it is plain that souls were not sent into bodies to chastise earlier sins, as those people prattle, but that God fashioned body and soul together, that is, the complete man. Therefore we await a recompense for the things done by us through the body, whether good or evil; for this is what the divine apostle Paul also teaches us, saying: For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things [done] through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (1 Cor. 5). The apostle's words must therefore be attended to: for he did not say that the one judged must receive according to what he did before the body. But if a man is either punished or deservedly rewarded by him who judges the earth only for the things he did through the body, and no mention is made of sins committed before, it is plain that souls do not exist before bodies. For if they pre-existed, the Apostle would have said: things done both through the body and before the body. That the souls of men use intelligence and reason is admitted; we think not even those who defend Origen deny this. Let those who agree with Origen tell us, then: their souls (if indeed, as they assert, they existed before bodies), before they entered them, in what rank were they, or what were they doing? For if they existed before, they ought to know where they were, or how they came here; but if they can in no way say this (for it is not true), it is clear that they are telling fables. But perhaps they may say that souls, after they have entered bodies, are then able to discern and recognise what they do. If they say this, it follows from their empty argument that the body has more worth and honour than the soul, since it gives it intelligence and reason by way of a favour; yet to assert this is full of madness and absurdity. And why, if the soul existed before the body, as they say, does it need teaching after it has come into the body, and is it instructed little by little and advances to better and more perfect things? For if it existed before, it would certainly know what is useful, and would need no teaching, nor, being as it were already engaged in knowledge, would it be educated by care and diligence; and if it knew what it is to stumble, it would not be taught what it had known before. But if it is taught, as one engaged in ignorance, it did not know before; if it did not know before, it did not exist before. And it is clear that it did not exist before. For God alone is the cause of our origin; who, as he made us when we did not exist, so protects and saves us, once born, by grace and by his own hand, if we are shown worthy and fit. For God, who said: Let us make man in our image and likeness (Gen. 1), made both together, that is, he formed the body and created the intelligent and rational soul. For at the same time he both shaped the body and founded the soul, presenting the complete man; for man is neither a body without a soul, nor a soul without a body. But if the soul pre-existed, as Origen raves, for what reason did the most holy prophet Zechariah say: Forming the spirit of man within him (Zech. 12)? For if it existed before, he ought rather to have said: Pouring the spirit of man into him as into a vessel, or sending it down into him. But since the prophet says 'forming', he shows that God, by his own power and goodness, made the soul, as also the body, not from things pre-existing. Since, then, man, as has been said, was made in the image and likeness of God, and was granted the divine inbreathing, it is plain from this that the soul was created not only intelligent and rational but also immortal, so that it should rule over all the things that were made on earth. For this is what was said of the soul by Gregory the Theologian: that it is from God, and divine, and a sharer in the nobility on high; not, as some suppose and say, that the soul is of the divine substance, but that, made by the inbreathing of God, it received grace from him to be intelligent, rational and immortal, and not to die together with the body, like the irrational animals, but by grace to be a sharer in the nobility on high, that is, in immortality. To this the holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, bears witness in the eleventh sermon on the creation; for he says thus (Homily 13 on Gen. 2): « And he breathed, it says, into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Here some unskilled men, moved by their own thoughts, and having nothing in mind befitting God, nor considering the condescension of the words, dare to say that the soul is from the substance of God. O insanity, O madness! » And this is what the Father [says] on the subject proposed. Consider, moreover, that of all the other things made on earth God said, Let there be, and Let the earth bring forth, and it was done (ibid.); but of man he says: Let us make man; and not only Let us make, but, in our image and likeness; and taking dust from the earth, he formed man with his own hands, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. From these things, then, it can be seen how God made man more honourable and more precious than all the other creatures that are on earth; all the others he made by a word: he spoke, and they were made; but man, as has been said, he made himself with his own hands, according to the divine Scripture; and whatever things were made by him on earth he subjected to man, who was made on the sixth day, so that he should rule over all earthly creatures, already made and prepared for him, while himself obeying the command of his maker. This too the holy Gregory the Theologian teaches us in the oration on New Sunday (Orat. 43); for he says thus: « So something is counted first among the days, and second, and third, and so on until the seventh day, on which there was rest from works; by these [days] are divided the things that are made, arranged by an ineffable plan, and not brought forth all at once by the all-powerful Word, for whom to think and to speak is to accomplish the thing itself. And if man was fashioned last, and that by the hand of God, and honoured with the image, it is no wonder; for, as for a king, it was fitting that the royal court should first be in place, and then the king be brought in, already escorted and guarded as it were by a retinue of all things. » Wherefore, if according to the teaching of Gregory the Theologian man was fashioned last, and that by the hand of God, and honoured with the image, and all things were prepared for him by God, and the palace was first in place for him as for a king, and so he was brought in by God, already escorted by the service of all things: how do those who are foolish after Origen say that pre-existent souls are sent down into bodies on account of sins, to pay for what they committed before? For on the contrary the holy Gregory says both that man was made last of all, and that he was honoured by God, and that he rules over all the things that are on earth: which is surely no sign of punishment, but of singular providence and kindness. With Gregory the Theologian, moreover, agrees the teaching of the holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, in the eleventh sermon on the creation, for he says thus (Hom. 13 on Genesis): « But perhaps someone may say: Why, if the soul is more precious than the body, is what is inferior made first, and only then what is greater and nobler? Do you not see, beloved, that this same thing was done in the creation itself? For just as heaven and earth and sun and moon and all the rest were fashioned, and last of all man, to whom the rule over all of them was to be entrusted, so in the forming of man the body is formed first, then the soul, which is more honourable. For as the creatures without reason, which were being prepared for his use and service, came into being before man, so that he who was to enjoy their benefits should have his services ready, so also the body was fashioned before the soul, so that when, according to the hidden wisdom of God, the soul was brought in, it might be able to carry out its proper functions by the movement of the body. » And this is enough to show those who hear that we everywhere think and say the same things as the Fathers, who do away with the pre-existence of souls. Moreover, since the holy Scripture says of Adam and Eve: God blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule over it (Gen. 1): how, if souls were older than bodies, was it going to be that, according to the divine command, those [souls] should increase and multiply which, according to their fables, existed before? And how could God bless souls already fallen into sins, so that they should increase and multiply? For souls defiled by sins were worthy of a curse rather than a blessing. And if souls pre-existed and, according to Origen's fables, were in another rank, why did God form Adam alone? Or had the soul of Adam alone sinned at that time, and was one body therefore fashioned by God? For if there were other souls before, other bodies ought to have been fashioned at the same time to receive the souls. And how was the soul, a sinner, as their reasoning has it, thrown into the body for punishment, placed by God in the paradise of delights? For if it had been sent into the body to pay a penalty, it would have been put not in that paradise but in a place of punishment. But God so greatly loved man, whom he had fashioned after all creatures, that when he had transgressed the commandment given him, and had for that reason been expelled from paradise, as the human race grew and sin spread, because the thought of man bent with depraved zeal towards worse things, God, being good, did not neglect his creature, but rebuked and chastised it in many ways, as the holy Scripture indicates. But after we needed a greater medicine for more grievous diseases, the only-begotten Word of God himself, one, that is, one person, of the holy Trinity, became man through his kindness, remaining God, neither his divine substance being turned into the human, nor the human changed into the divine; and he is one and the same in both natures, and is recognised in them without confusion and without division. For remaining what he was, he became what he was not; and taking upon himself in his own flesh the death owed by us from the condemnation of the transgression, he freed us from eternal death, having become the firstfruits of those who sleep, and, rising as the firstborn from the dead, he raised us up with him and made us sit with him in the heavenly places (1 Cor. 15; Col. 1; Eph. 2), as the apostolic tradition teaches us. For although from the beginning human nature was deprived of paradise because of disobedience, yet, as has been said, the only-begotten Son of God, because of his great love with which he loved us (Eph. 2), uniting our nature to himself indivisibly according to hypostasis in the womb of the holy, glorious Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, deigned [to grant] us a greater grace, giving us the kingdom of heaven. And to this the holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, bears witness in the sermon on the Ascension (vol. 3 of his works), saying thus: « We who had proved unworthy of the earth have today been raised into heaven; we who had not been worthy even of a lower dominion have ascended to the kingdom on high, passing beyond the heavens and attaining the royal throne. The nature on account of which the Cherubim guarded paradise (Gen. 3) itself today sits above the Cherubim. » Therefore it has been shown that souls were not first in the heavens, as Origen prattles, and then sent into bodies to pay the penalty for sins committed; but on the contrary that the whole human nature, fashioned on earth, that is, body and soul, has attained the heavens by divine goodness and favour, so that those men who kept and fulfilled the commandment of God should be held worthy of the company of the angels in the heavens, whom we have been commanded to imitate on earth through confession towards God. For since God, because of his unspeakable love for mankind, wished that, as he is glorified in the heavens by the holy powers, so he should also be glorified on earth by men, he fashioned man, another angel on earth, so that all things should be filled with the glory of God. And so the Lord, teaching how one should pray, says: Our Father, who are in the heavens, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done as in heaven, so also on earth.

Moreover, with what has been said by us agree the things which the holy Gregory the Theologian teaches in his sermon on holy Easter (Orat. 42, which is the 2nd on Easter); for he speaks thus: « When the Word, the craftsman, wished to display this thing, he fashions also one living creature out of both, that is, out of the visible and the invisible nature, [namely] man; and taking a body from matter which already existed before, and putting life into it from himself (which reason certainly knows to be the intelligent soul and the image of God), he set him on earth as a kind of second world, great in small, another angel, a worshipper of mixed [nature], a beholder of the visible nature, and an initiate of that which is grasped by the mind alone; ruler of the things on earth, obedient to the rule from above. » Therefore it must be noted that this Father, when he said that God made man out of both, added that the body was taken from matter that existed before; but he did not say that the soul existed before, nor that it was born from any substance which existed before, but that God by himself put in life, which reason knows to be the intelligent soul and the image of God. And what the Father says, that God made man ruler on earth, bound to the rule from above, overturns the assertion of those who say that souls were sent into bodies for punishment. For to reign on earth and to be held under the rule of God alone is not to be counted as a place of punishment, but as a great benefit and gift of God.

In addition to this we think we must necessarily say this against those who assert pre-existence: If it were true that souls exist before bodies, they would know and remember what they had done before they came into bodies, just as after death they know and are aware of what they did in their bodies. And we shall show that the soul after its departure from life knows what it did, from the very words of the Gospel; for our Lord and Saviour Christ says this in the Gospel according to Luke, in the passage about Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 19): There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, longing to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table; and even the dogs came and licked his sores. And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by angels into the bosom of Abraham. And the rich man also died, and was buried. And in hell, lifting up his eyes when he was in torments, he saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus in his bosom; and he cried out and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. And besides all these things, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross over to you cannot, nor cross from there to here. And he said: I ask you then, father, to send him to my father's house; for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments. Therefore let those who defend Origen be ashamed, at least by the words of the holy Gospel. For if souls had existed before bodies, they would know what they had done before the body, just as after their departure from life they remember what they did in the body; for this we learn from the words of the holy Gospel.

That the holy Fathers too, following the divinely inspired Scriptures, condemned such a doctrine together with Origen who devised it, we have already clearly shown from what they said; nevertheless we shall demonstrate it also from the following testimonies of the Fathers. And first we shall put forward the holy Peter, who was bishop of Alexandria and a martyr, bearing witness to these words of ours.

Of St Peter, bishop of Alexandria and martyr, from the first sermon, that the soul did not pre-exist, nor, having sinned, was for that reason sent into a body: « We have thought that certain things should be set out concerning the first earthly man from the earth, so as to show that one and the same [man] was made at one and the same time, although sometimes the inner and the outer man are spoken of separately. For even if, according to the saving word, he who made the inner things made the outer things too, yet [he made them] once and at the same time, that is, on the same day, when God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness; from which it is clear that [man] was not made by a coming together, as if something else had gone before and had come together from another place. For if there was a coming together, why was what had already been made described? » And after other things: « So it is not accepted that souls sin in heaven before bodies, [souls] which did not exist at all even before bodies; for this doctrine is from the philosophy of the pagans, which is foreign, and alien to those who wish to live piously in Christ. »

Of the same, from the mystagogy which he delivered to the Church when he was about to receive the crown of martyrdom: « Therefore I beseech you, be watchful. For you are about to face affliction again. You know what dangers were undergone by my father and bishop Theonas, who raised me, at the hands of those who were mad for idols: to whose see I succeeded, would that also to his ways! You know how greatly Dionysius conducted himself, who hid himself from place to place, while Sabellius moreover afflicted [him]. What, further, shall I say of Heraclas and Demetrius, the blessed bishops? What trials they endured from the mad Origen, since he sowed dissensions in the Church which stir up disturbances in it to this very day! » Can anyone, then, of those who think rightly oppose what has been said against Origen by the holy martyr and bishop of Alexandria, Peter? He, undertaking the noble contest for Christ, not only renounced Origen and his wicked doctrine, but also testifies that the holy Fathers who had been before him endured many trials from that man's madness.

The holy Athanasius too, who was himself also bishop of Alexandria, said in his sermon on the life of the blessed Antony: « How do you dare to mock us, who say that Christ was manifested as man? When you, defining the soul as [coming] from mind, say that it went astray and fell from the vault of heaven into a body? » Let those who hear note that the holy Athanasius openly opposes those who say that mind pre-exists, and that from it the soul arose, which defiled itself with sin and fell from the vault of heaven into a body.

Of the same St Athanasius, from the second sermon against the Arians: « Every visible creature was made in six days; and on the first day light, which he called day; on the second the firmament; on the third, having gathered the waters, he revealed the dry land and brought forth various fruits on it; on the fourth he made the sun and moon and the whole choir of stars; on the fifth he established the generation of the swimming things of the sea and the flying things of the air; on the sixth he made the four-footed beasts on the earth, and finally man, who is of a rational soul and a body. And his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made (Rom. 1); and neither is light like night, nor the sun like the moon, nor angels like thrones, nor these like powers; but all are indeed creatures, yet each of the things that have come into being persists and remains according to its kind in its own substance, as it was made. » See, the holy Athanasius too teaches that after all creatures God made man of a body and an intelligent and rational soul. For he did not say that the body was made after all things, so that a pre-existing soul might enter into it; but he said that after all creatures man was made, who is of a rational soul and a body, showing that God fashioned both, that is, body and soul, together.

And since Origen added this to his other blasphemies, that the soul of the Lord existed before, and that God the Word was united to it before he was made flesh from the Virgin, the holy Athanasius himself, overturning this delusion too in his letter to Epictetus, speaks thus: « Rightly will all condemn themselves who think that the flesh which is from Mary existed before Mary, and that God the Word had a human soul before her, and was always in it before the coming. » Therefore if, from what was said by the holy Athanasius, the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was made like us in all things without sin, did not exist before his coming in the flesh, what madness is it to say that other souls of men exist before bodies?

Let us hear besides St Basil in the sermon on that [text] (Hom. 16): « In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God », speaking thus: « See that the ambiguity of the word never deceives you; for how was human reason in the beginning, when man received the beginning of his generation last? Before man there were wild beasts, before man beasts of burden; creeping things, both of land and of water; the birds of heaven, the stars, the sun, the moon; grass, earth, sea, heaven. » See, the Father plainly warns us not to be led on by the fables of Origen about the pre-existence of souls. For he teaches us [that some suppose] human reason, that is the soul, to have been in the beginning; but he plainly cries out that the origin of men is later than all the creatures of God. If then all creatures were before man, how did souls exist before? For the Father says that all things existed not before the body, but before man, who is soul and body; from which it is shown that both were fashioned together.

The holy Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, also says in the Disputation on Man (ch. 28): « And perhaps it is not foreign to the purpose of our discussion to weigh what is disputed in the Churches concerning soul and body. For some of those who were before us, who published a treatise on first principles, hold that souls previously subsisted like a kind of people in a city of their own, and that there examples both of virtue and of wickedness were set before them; and that the soul which remained in virtue and uprightness never experiences union with and struggle against a body; but if it fell away from participation in the good, it slips down into this life, and so comes to be in a body. Others, attending to the order of man's creation from Moses, say that the soul is later in time than the body, since God first took clay from the earth and formed man, and then gave him life by breathing into him. » And a little after: « Those who defend the first account, and assert a city, as it were, of souls more ancient than bodily life, do not seem to me to be free of the fables of the pagans which have been handed down about the migration of souls from some bodies into others. For if anyone examines it closely, he will find that their account necessarily comes down to this. They say that one of the wise men of their sect said that he had been both a man and had put on a woman's body, and had flown up with the birds, and had been a shrub, and had been allotted a life in the water. In my judgement at least, he who affirms these things of himself does not stray far from the truth. For truly a teaching of this kind, which says that one soul passes through so many things, is worthy of the chattering noise of frogs or jackdaws, or the irrationality of fishes, or the insensibility of trees. And the cause of these absurdities is this, that they supposed souls to pre-exist. For the principle of such a doctrine, advancing consequentially to what is akin and connected, extends its inventions this far. For if the soul, drawn down from a higher life through vices, becomes man, and if it is admitted that bodily life is more subject to passions than the eternal and incorporeal, it is necessary that the soul, living in this life, in which more opportunities for sinning are at hand, should be involved in more vices and be more affected by passions. But passion in the human soul is a likeness to the irrational. Bound therefore to this life, the soul will slip down into the nature of beasts, and having once entered upon vices, and dwelling in irrationality, it will set no end to its progress in wickedness. For where wickedness halts, an impulse toward virtue follows; but there is no virtue in irrational beings; it will therefore necessarily be changed for the worse, constantly advancing to worse and baser things, and always devising whatever is lower than the nature in which it is. Further, just as the sentient lies below the rational, so from this too there is a falling away to the insentient. Wherefore their account, issuing in this, strays from the truth, and by a kind of consequence betakes itself from absurdities to absurdities. Thereafter their doctrine proceeds fabulously through things that do not cohere with one another. But the consequence itself shows the complete corruption of the soul. For the soul that has once fallen from the higher life sets no limit to its wickedness; but because of the custom and habit of the passions it will come down from the rational to the irrational, and thence it will be changed into the insensibility of plants; and upon the insentient follows the inanimate, upon the inanimate that which does not subsist. And so, entirely by this consequence, the soul will for them finally pass into non-being. Thus it will have no means of returning to better things. But in fact they bring the soul back from a shrub to a man; therefore they show that the life in a shrub is more excellent than the incorporeal life. For it has already been shown that the soul's progress is toward the worse, and therefore toward the lower; and the inanimate lies below the insentient nature, to which by consequence the principle of their doctrine reduces the soul. But since this is known, either they shut the soul up in the insentient, or, if they bring it back from there to human life, they show, as was said, that the life led in a plant surpasses the first state of souls, since from that there was a falling away to wickedness, but from this there is a return to virtue. Wherefore that account is proved to be without head and without end which asserts that souls live separately before bodily life, and are bound to bodies because of their misdeeds. » Thus the Nyssene. Since then the teaching of this Father is plain, and condemns those who say that souls existed before bodies, let us hear also the holy Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from a sermon written to certain monks who agreed with Origen; for he speaks thus: « Wherefore anathematize Origen and the other heretics, after our example, and that of Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, renowned from former contests, was made leader of a most noble people, whom the whole synod of the blessed bishops of the West also follows, which received and approved the sentence of the Church of the Alexandrians passed against the impious man. »

From the same, from the letter to the saints who were in Scetis, on account of those who found fault with the condemnation of Origen's doctrine: « Some have dared to say that Origen is a teacher of the Church. Are these, I ask you, to be borne? If Origen is a teacher of the Church, the Arians and Eunomians and pagans take great airs upon themselves: the former blaspheming against the Son and the Spirit; the latter likewise impious, as those are, and also mocking the resurrection of the dead. » From this it is clear that he who follows the holy Fathers does not doubt that those who think with Origen follow the error of the pagans and the madness of the Arians.

The holy Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, also says this in the letter to the monks who were in Phua, against those who affirm that there is no resurrection of bodies: « They say, then, that there are among you some who deny the resurrection of human bodies, which is part of our confession, which we made when approaching saving baptism. For in professing the faith we add that we also believe in the resurrection of the flesh. If we take this away, and do not believe that Christ rose from the dead so as to raise us up with himself, we have held a limping faith, and, turning aside from the royal road, we follow a crooked path. And an evil opinion of this kind is from the madness of Origen, whom our fathers also renounced and anathematized as a corrupter of the truth. For he did not think as a Christian, but, following the absurdities and trifles of the pagans, he fell into error. And here is where the beginning of his sickness came to him. He asserts that souls exist before bodies, and that they were drawn away from holiness into desires and wickedness, and rebelled against God, by whom for this reason they were condemned and bound to a body, and are in the flesh as in a prison. »

From the same, from the letter written to the monks who were in Phua: « But the Church, obedient to the Scriptures inspired by God, neither knows that the soul existed before bodies, nor that it sinned before them. For how could that which did not subsist sin? But we affirm that the maker of the universe formed the body from earth and gave it life with an intelligent soul, and this is the structure of man. » And after other things: « That the soul of man was neither condemned for past misdeeds and crimes, as they say, nor sent down into this world, the most wise Paul makes credible, writing thus: For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things [done] through the body, according to what he did, whether good or evil (1 Cor. 15). Why then does he say that we must be made manifest only on account of the things proper to the body, and not rather also on account of those before the body, if he knew that the soul existed before and sinned before? But if we are brought to judgement on account of those things alone which we did in the body, we certainly do not have a sin older than the body; for the soul of man did not at all exist before it. Moreover the force of the letter of the law also makes this plain. For if, as the wandering Origen says, the soul received the body in place of punishment and penalty for former offences, why has it threatened death to the wicked and criminal? For it would rather have been fitting for good and just men to meet death, so that they might be freed from bonds and punishment; and on the contrary for the criminal and impious to live, so that they might be punished, and there might be no release from their bonds. »

From the exposition of the synodical letter of the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria against the doctrine of Origen: « This Origen, then, of whom we are treating, stood forth like the abomination of desolation in the midst of the true Church; and, ordained presbyter by a canonical, a single, a true hand, he held the bare and mere dignity of presbyter, just as the thief and traitor Judas also held the honour of apostleship. For when he had begun to deliver blasphemous homilies, Heraclas of blessed memory, then bishop, as a lover of the truth, a ploughman and vinedresser of the Church's field, pulled him out from the midst of the fine and flourishing crop, because he was in truth of the evil tares. » And a little after: « Wherefore he, falling from heaven to earth like lightning, as did his father the devil also, breathing much and savage wrath against the truth, sailed to the region of Palestine; and staying in the metropolis of the Caesareans, when he had put off the mask he had assumed and revealed himself, like the fish which some call the cuttlefish, he showed what pleased him, and vomiting forth the dark and black poison of life, he set it down there in writing, and like a Jewish tavern-keeper, under the appearance and pretence of good, he mixed bitter with sweet. For what does this man say, scheming wickedly and raving? The soul, he says, existed before the body, and pre-existed in the heavens; and when it had sinned there, God plunged it into custody, that is, sent it down into a body, for the purging, he says, and chastisement of the crimes committed in the heavens. From here at once this most impious man first tells his fables and strives to fight against the truth. » And a little after: « If the soul existed before in the heavens, and first sinned there, as the unsound Origen, fighting against God, said, the most holy prophet ought not to have said: And forming the spirit of man within him (Zech. 12), but rather: Plunging the spirit of man within him, as into a wineskin; or perhaps: Sending down. But now since he does not say this, but 'forming within him', he shows that this man is a most grievous wolf, clothed outwardly in a sheep's skin for a deceit of destruction. For as though coming from heaven and clearly knowing the things established there, the senseless man says not only that the soul pre-existed, but also that it sinned before. » Therefore it has been demonstrated both from divine Scripture and from the holy Fathers that the imaginings of the heretics about the pre-existence of souls agree neither with the true faith of Christians nor with right reason.

Moreover, this too shows the madness of Origen, that he affirms that the heaven, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the waters which are above the heavens, are ensouled, and are certain powers that use reason. But the holy Basil openly refutes these things in the third homily of his commentaries on the Hexaemeron, arguing thus against the doctrine of Origen (near the end): « Further, we must speak about the separated waters, and to those who have fallen away from the Church, who, under the pretext of an anagogical sense and, forsooth, of loftier meanings, have taken refuge in allegory, and assert that certain spiritual and incorporeal powers are signified figuratively by the waters; and that the better ones remained above in the firmament, while the worse ones stayed below in earthly and wild places; and for this reason, they say, the waters which are above the heavens praise the Lord, that is, the good powers, which are worthy, because of the purity of their better part, to render fitting praise to the Creator; but the waters which are beneath the heavens are the spirits of wickedness, which fell from their natural height into the depth of evil; and these, as turbulent and seditious, and tossing with the tumults of the passions, are called seas, because of the easy change and instability of their voluntary motions. But let us reject reasonings of this kind as confused dreams and old wives' tales; let us think that water is water, and accept the separation made from the firmament according to the reason given. And if ever the waters which are above the heavens (Ps. 148) are summoned to the glorification of the common Lord of all things, let us not on that account say that they are a nature that uses reason. For the heavens are not ensouled because they tell the glory of God (Ps. 18), nor is the firmament endowed with an animal's sense because it proclaims the works of his hands. » So far Basil. Further, the hearers must take note that the Father, in using that manner of speaking, « We have a word to those who are from the Church, » is discussing Origen, expelled from the grace of God and from the holy Church of God, and his followers: for he did not say « to those who are in the Church », but « We have a word to those who are from the Church »; and by saying « we » he signified the men of the Church, while by « those who are from the Church » he denoted those cast out from it.

But the one and only zeal of the impious Origen was to confirm the error of the pagans and to sow tares in the souls of the weaker. Therefore we have decided to add this too, which is truly worthy of laughter, yet was said by him, concerning the resurrection of men from the dead. He affirmed that in the resurrection the bodies of men are raised spherical. O the madness and ignorance of a man insane, an expounder of the pagans' learning! Blind in mind and eager to mix fables with the faith of Christians, he strove to violate with insult the very hope and salvation of Christians, that is, the resurrection promised to us, not even revering the resurrection of the Lord. For the Lord, rising from the dead and made the firstfruits of those who sleep (John 20), was seen by the disciples, and showed them the holes in his hands and feet and the wound in his side; and after the resurrection he ate, not as needing food, but in order thereby to confirm the nature of the raised body. And indeed, when the Lord ascended, the angels said to the disciples: This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1). But if, as Origen raves, the body of the Lord was spherical, how could he show the holes in his hands and feet, or the wound in his side? Or how could he eat, or be recognised by the disciples at all? And in what way could the bodies of the saints which rose after the Lord's resurrection (Matt. 27) and appeared in the holy city be recognised by others, if they were in a different shape from what they had had in life? Since, then, the impious Origen was in no way established on the rock of faith, but had put forth blasphemies of this kind and far more atrocious than these, it is no wonder that at the very moment of martyrdom he denied Christ and worshipped the multitude of gods honoured by the pagans, which he himself introduces. And this happened by the providence of God, so that he should not be received in the Church as a martyr, and some harm thereby be brought upon the flock of Christ. For if even now there are some who acknowledge his fall yet defend his doctrine, would they not have defended it as that of a martyr and a Father, had it happened that he was perfected without showing any worship to idols? For no one who holds fast to the truth falls away from God or is forsaken by him, according to what the divine Scripture says: Look, children, at the generations of men, and you will know that no one has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame. For who has remained in his commandments and been forsaken? Or who has called upon him, and he despised him (Sir. 2)? But the impious Origen did not confine his blasphemies to himself, but by his own writings passed on his error to many others, so that the saying of the holy apostle Paul fits him very well, which says: The sins of some men are manifest, going before to judgement; but some they also follow after (1 Tim. 5). For the succession of his error, creeping into the souls of the weaker, causes the sins committed by him from the beginning to follow him.

For as if the impiety concerning the pre-existence of souls, and the rest of his idle talk and his blasphemies concerning the holy Trinity, were not enough for those who follow the opinions of Origen, they add this too to their own error, having his perverse teaching as their guide and author, so that they say that the punishment of all impious men, and moreover of the demons, will have an end, and that both impious men and demons will be restored to their former rank. In saying this they make men slack in carrying out the commandments of God, turning them away from the narrow and strait way and leading them into the error of the broad and spacious one. And they altogether oppose the words of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ; for he himself teaches in the holy Gospel that the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life (Matt. 25); and again he says to those on the right: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; but to those on the left: Depart from me, accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (ibid.). Since, then, the Lord in the holy Gospel openly proclaims both an unceasing punishment and an unceasing kingdom, it is clear that these men prefer the ravings of Origen to the sayings of the Lord. From this too their madness is refuted. For if anyone, following his trifles, holds that punishment will cease, he must also set an end to the eternal life promised to the just; for 'eternal' is applied equally in both. But if both punishment and the enjoyment of glory have an end, why was there the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ? Why the crucifixion, and the death, and the burial, and the resurrection of the Lord? What benefit is there for those who have fought the good fight and undergone martyrdom for Christ, if both the demons and impious men are going to have, by restoration, the same rank as the saints? But let this be turned upon the heads of those who tell such fables. For the words of Christ remain unshaken in the minds of the faithful, and in the very truth of things.

Further, those who defend the wicked opinion of Origen, fleeing these firm arguments and trying to cover their error, take certain sayings of the holy Fathers wrongly and, interpreting them perversely according to their own opinion, accommodate them to their own sickness; which they also do with the divine Scriptures. But we shall show from the holy Fathers themselves that their reasonings are empty and futile. The holy Gregory the Theologian, then, writes thus in his apologetic oration: « But for us, for whom the salvation of a blessed and immortal soul is at stake, a soul which will enter upon either everlasting punishment or praise on account of its wickedness or virtue, how highly must this contest be valued, or how much knowledge is needed? » And after a little: « By what false defence, by what artful persuasion, by what invention fighting against the truth, will justice be circumvented and right judgement deceived, which places all things for all men in the balance, deeds, words and all thoughts, and weighs what was wickedly committed against what was better, so that whichever side tips the scale prevails, and sentence is pronounced according to the greater part, a sentence which no appeal can set aside, no higher judge, no defence of other deeds, no oil taken either from the wise virgins (Matt. 25) or from those who sell to those whose lamps are failing, no repentance of the rich man tormented in the flame (Luke 16) and seeking the amendment of his kinsmen, no appointed day for change: but a justice sure and fixed, and fearful, and final, and more equitable and just than it is terrible, or rather terrible because of its justice, when the thrones are set, and the Ancient of Days sits, and the books are opened, and the river of fire is drawn out, and light is before him, and darkness prepared; and those who have done good go to the resurrection of life (John 3), which is now hidden in Christ but afterwards appears with him; but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement; and those who do not believe this have already been judged and condemned by the Word, which has judged them; and some the ineffable light receives, and the grace of the holy and reigning Trinity, shining forth more openly and purely and mingling itself wholly with the whole mind, which alone I consider to be the kingdom of heaven; but others, along with other evils, torment, or rather, before all others, to have been cast away from God, and shame of conscience and disgrace that has no end. »

Of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, from his book of Rules. Question: If [the Lord] says that one will be beaten with many stripes, another with few (Luke 12), how do some say that there will be no end of punishment for those who are punished? Answer: Things which are ambiguous and seem to be said obscurely in some places of the divinely inspired Scripture are made clear elsewhere by other passages which are acknowledged and plain. Since, then, the Lord has pronounced: These will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life (Matt. 25); and in one place sends [some] into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels; and elsewhere names the Gehenna of fire, and adds: Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9); and again foretold through the prophet concerning certain people: Their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched (Isa. 66); since these and similar things are often set forth by the divinely inspired Scripture, this too is one of the devil's arts and cunning, that many men, as if forgetting such great sayings of the Lord, dare to sketch out for themselves an end of the punishments of sin in the future. For if the eternal punishment is at some time to have an end, eternal life too will certainly have an end; if we do not take the sense of the Gospel saying thus in the case of life, what reason is there to set an end to eternal punishment? For the addition of 'eternal' is placed equally in both. For these, he says, will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life (Matt. 25). Of the same, from the homily exhorting to holy baptism: « For the brief and temporary pleasure of sin I am tormented with everlasting punishment; for the pleasure of the flesh I am consigned to eternal fire. » Of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, from the first letter to Theodore the monk: « Keep these things constantly in mind, and the river of fire: For a fiery and swift river came forth from his face (Dan. 7). There is no reason for anyone given over to that fire to expect an end of punishment. But the wicked pleasures of this world differ in nothing from shadows and dreams; for before the sin has reached its end, the pleasure is extinguished; but of the punishments undergone for crimes there is no end. » Of the same, from the commentaries on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: « No slight question is set before us here, but one about very necessary matters. All men ask whether the fire of Gehenna will have an end: the Lord has declared that it will not, when he said: Their fire will not be quenched and their worm will not die (Mark 9). And Paul, showing it to be everlasting, says: Sinners will pay the penalty in eternal destruction (2 Thess. 1). » Therefore, since the divine Scripture and the holy Fathers teach us that there is no end of the punishment of the impious and of the demons who are worshipped by them, what restoration do those who think with Origen imagine, where there is no way out of punishments! For the holy Church of Christ, just as it proclaims unceasing eternal life for the just, so it teaches that punishments await the impious perpetually. And so much on these matters. Further, we have judged that a few out of the many authorities of the divine Scripture and the holy Fathers should be brought forward to refute the impiety of the Origenists.

Since, however, we wish to drive every stumbling-block out of the most holy Church, so that no stain may be left in it, we, following the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, who struck down Origen himself and his wicked and impious doctrine of this kind and rightly subjected [them] to anathema, have sent this letter to your Beatitude. By it we urge [you] to hold an assembly of all the most holy bishops now staying in this royal city, and of the most God-beloved heads of the holy monasteries that are here, and to see that all of them in writing anathematize in every way the aforesaid impious Origen, opposed to God, who is also [called] Adamantius, who was a presbyter of the most holy Church of Alexandria, and his wicked and impious doctrines, and all the chapters which are set out below. And you are to send copies of what has been done by your Beatitude on this account to all the other most holy bishops and heads of the venerable monasteries, so that they too by their own signature may anathematize Origen and his wicked doctrines, together with all the heretics who will be declared. And for the future, let no bishops or heads of monasteries be ordained otherwise than if they first anathematize, together with all the other heretics who are customarily anathematized in the published declarations, that is, Sabellius, Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy Aelurus, and Peter Mongus, and Anthimus of Trebizond, Theodosius of Alexandria, Peter who was [bishop] of Antioch, and Peter of Apamea, and Severus formerly of Antioch, also the aforesaid Origen, who suffered from the madness of the pagans and the Arians, together with his accursed and impious doctrines. For all must be told beforehand that no one at all should dare to defend such a heretic or his expositions, but that each should hate, shun and anathematize them with his whole soul and his whole thought, as foreign to the Christian tradition and bringing a grievous plague and pestilence to the souls of the simpler.

These same things we have written not only to your Holiness but also to the most holy and most blessed pope and patriarch of elder Rome, Vigilius, and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs, that is, of Alexandria, Theopolis and Jerusalem, so that they too may attend to this matter and that it may be brought to its conclusion. And since we desire that all Christians should know that the writings of Origen are altogether foreign to the true faith of Christians, we have decided that out of his many and immense blasphemies a few should be set down word for word. They run as follows.
That the Son is less than the Father, and the Spirit than the Son, from the first book of Peri Archon.

That God the Father, holding all things together, reaches to each one of the things that are, imparting being to each from his own; for he is being. The Son, being less than the Father, reaches to rational beings alone; for he is second to the Father. Still less is the Holy Spirit, reaching to the saints alone. So in this respect the power of the Father is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that of the Son greater than that of the Holy Spirit, and again the power of the Holy Spirit is more excellent than that of the other holy beings.
That the power of God the Father is finite, from the second book of the same work.

For it must be said that the power of God too is finite, and its limitation must not be removed on the pretext of praise. And a little later: For he made as many things as he could grasp and hold under his hand and keep under his providence; just as he also constructed as much matter as he could administer and adorn.
Of the same, from the fourth book of the same work.

Let no one be offended by the statement if we have set a limit even to the power of God. For to embrace infinite things is by nature impossible; for since the things which God himself comprehends are once and for all finite, there must be a limit to how many finite things he is sufficient for.
That the Son is a creature and made, from the same book.

This Son, begotten of the will of the Father, who is the image of the invisible God, and the radiance of his glory, and the express image of his substance, the firstborn of all creation, a creature, wisdom (Col. 1; Heb. 1; 1 Cor. 5). For Wisdom herself says: The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works (Prov. 9).

But if the Father contains all things, and the Son is of the number of all things, it is clear that he too is contained. Someone else may ask whether it is true that God is known by himself equally as by the Only-begotten; and he will assert that that saying is true in all respects: The Father who sent me is greater than I (John 10 and 14). Therefore in being understood too the Father is understood more fully, more clearly and more perfectly by himself than by the Son.
From the first volume of the same book.
Therefore we, made after the image, have the Son, as being the truth, as the exemplar of the beautiful formations in us. And what we are to the Son himself, he is to the Father, who is the truth.
Of the same, from the same book.

Thus therefore I think it can fittingly be said of the Saviour too that he is the image of God's goodness, but not goodness itself; perhaps the Son is also good, but not good simply. And just as he is the image of the invisible God, and for that reason God, yet not he of whom Christ himself says: That they may know you, the only true God (John 17), so he is the image of goodness, yet not unchangeably [good] as the Father [is].

That, calling the Son together with the Holy Spirit a creature, he counted them among the other creatures; and for that reason called them ministering living creatures, from the fourth book of Peri Archon.

That, therefore, everything other than the Father and God of all things has been created, we are persuaded by the same line of reasoning. And after a little: The Hebrew said that those two seraphim in Isaiah, having six wings, crying one to the other and saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts (Jer. 6), are the only-begotten of God and the Holy Spirit. And we think that what is found in the song of Habakkuk also: In the midst of the two living creatures you will be known (Hab. 3), is to be referred to Christ and the Holy Spirit.
From the second book of Peri Archon: that he calls a mere man Lord.

For this reason Christ too was made man, having obtained this by his own merit, as the prophet testifies, saying: You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows (Prov. 44). For it was fitting that he who was never separated from the Only-begotten should coexist with the Only-begotten and be glorified together with him.
That creatures are coeternal with God, from the first book of Peri Archon.

For how would it not be absurd that God, from not having some one of the things that befit him, should come to have [it]? Since, then, he was never not almighty, those things on account of which he is almighty must be eternal. They were therefore always subject to his dominion, having him as ruler.
From the same book.

All genera and species always were; one would not say so of individuals that differ in number. Yet from both it is made clear that God did not make a beginning of creating, as though he had once been idle.
On the pre-existence of souls, from the first book of Peri Archon.

Through the fault of those who do not attend to themselves watchfully, falls occur sooner or later, and that either for longer or for shorter periods; so that the divine judgement, for this reason, measures out a fitting recompense to the good or evil movements of each. This one, in the future ordering of the world, will have the angelic rank, or the power of a principality, or authority over some, or a throne over subjects of a kingdom, or dominion over servants. Those who have not fallen far will have the administration and assistance we have spoken of. And so, for the most part, out of those who are under the principalities and powers and thrones and dominions, perhaps at some time the human race will also be established in their place in one world.
From the same book: that if demons are changed for the better, they will at some time make up human nature.

And I think that out of those who are subject to the worse principalities and powers and world-rulers in the several worlds, or minds of some world receiving benefit more quickly and willing thereafter to be changed by them, the human race may at some time be made up.
On him who, made from above, has fallen into a body.

So since the world consists of the greatest variety and contains so great a difference among rational beings, what else must be said to have been the cause of its existing than the various modes of falling of those who flow down from the unity not alike? And sometimes the soul chooses an aquatic life.
From the second book of Peri Archon.

The soul, flowing down from the good and inclining to wickedness, and embracing it for a long time, unless it brings itself back from folly, passes into beasts of burden and grows wild because of its depravity. And a little later: And it chooses to become brutish, even, so to speak, an aquatic life. And perhaps, according to the desert of its greater lapse into vice, it puts on the aquatic bodies of such a brute animal.
From the same book: that there will be a complete laying aside of bodies.

But if the things subjected to Christ are at last subjected also to God, bodies will be laid aside by all (1 Cor. 15); and I think that there will then be a dissolution into non-being; the nature of bodies will begin to exist again if rational beings descend once more.
From the third book of the same treatise, on the same subject.

Since God is said to become all in all (ibid.), just as we cannot assert [that he becomes] wickedness, so God does not become all in all, nor what brute beasts are, lest God become what wickedness is, and what brute beasts are; nor what inanimate things are, lest when God becomes all things he become also what they are: so neither [does he become] what bodies are, which by their own nature are in the soul.
From the second book of Peri Archon.

From the fact that it fell away and grew cold, that is, suffered what in Greek is called psyxis [cooling], away from the spiritual life, it became what is now the soul, in Greek psyche; and it admits also of a return to that which it was from the beginning. This I think is signified by the prophet when he says: Return, my soul, to your rest (Ps. 119), so that the whole of this is mind. Mind, then, became soul, and soul, restored by right deeds, becomes mind.
From the same book, on the same subject.
