Just as the Saviour came to save what had perished (Luke 19), and that which had perished, once it is saved, is no longer said to have perished, so the soul which he came to save, so that he might save what had perished, is no longer soul once it has been saved, nor can it be said to have perished, as it could be said before. This must still be weighed: whether, just as what perished was once a thing that had not perished, and there will be a time when it will not be a thing that has perished, so also the soul was once not soul, and there will be a time when it will not be soul.
From the fourth book.

It is necessary that the nature of bodies is not pre-existent, but subsists at intervals on account of certain falls, of rational beings that surround things and need bodies; and that when perfect amendment has been made, these are dissolved again into nothing, so that this happens forever.
From the first volume of the same book: that the sun and moon and stars are animate.
Moreover, that the soul of the sun is older than its binding to the body has already been concluded from the comparison of man with it; but I think this can also be shown from the Scriptures.
From the same book.

It is better to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1), for this is much better. The sun too, I think, would say this very thing: It is better to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for this is much better. For the rest, Paul says: But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (ibid.); the sun, however, would say: But to remain in this heavenly body is more necessary for the sake of the revelation of the sons of God. The same must be said of the moon and the other stars.
From the fourth volume of the same book: that Christ must be crucified for the demons too, and this many times through the ages to come.

And yet if anyone raises a question even about the passion itself, he will surely seem to be boldly inquiring into this with respect to the heavenly places. But if in the heavenly places there are spiritual forces of wickedness, then just as here we are certainly not ashamed to confess [him] crucified in order to destroy what he destroyed by suffering, so, granting that something similar happens there too, and the rest until the consummation of the whole age, we shall fear nothing.
From the same book.
Who of sound mind would hold that the first, second and third day, and evening and morning, existed without sun, moon and stars?
These things being so, then, and all Origen's blasphemies having been made public, it is fitting that the anathema against him be pronounced thus.

I. If anyone says or thinks that the souls of men pre-exist, as having formerly been minds and holy powers, and that they became sated with divine contemplation and turned to the worse, and for this reason grew cold from the love of God, and hence were called psychai in Greek, that is, souls, and were sent down into bodies by way of punishment: let him be anathema.
II. If anyone says or thinks that the soul of the Lord existed beforehand and was united to God the Word before the incarnation and the birth from the Virgin: let him be anathema.

III. If anyone says or thinks that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the womb of the blessed Virgin, and that afterwards God the Word and the soul, as having existed before, were united to it: let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone says or thinks that God the Word was made like all the heavenly orders, and became a cherub for the cherubim and a seraph for the seraphim, and was made entirely like all the powers above: let him be anathema.
V. If anyone says or thinks that in the resurrection the bodies of men are raised spherical, and does not confess that we are raised upright: let him be anathema.
VI. If anyone says that the heaven, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the waters that are above the heavens are certain animate and material [rational] powers: let him be anathema.
VII. If anyone says or thinks that the Lord Christ will be crucified in the age to come for the demons, as also for men: let him be anathema.
VIII. If anyone says or thinks either that the power of God is limited, or that he made as many things as he was able to comprehend: let him be anathema.

IX. If anyone says or thinks that the punishment of demons and of impious men is temporary, and that it will at some time have an end, or that there will be a restoration and reintegration of demons or impious men: let him be anathema.

Anathema also to Origen, also called Adamantius, who set out these things, together with his abominable, accursed and wicked doctrine, and to anyone who thinks these things, or defends them, or in any way whatever at any time presumes to uphold them.
Letter of the emperor Justinian to the holy synod of Constantinople concerning Origen and his followers.

Our concern has been and is to keep the holy Church of God and the apostles safe from disturbances, as is right, and to condemn whatever things are found in any way [to be] against the orthodox [faith].

Since, then, we have learned that there are at Jerusalem certain monks who follow and teach the impious errors of Pythagoras, Plato and Origen Adamantius, we thought that care and inquiry should be applied to them, lest they should in the end destroy many with their pagan and Manichaean impostures. For they say (to mention a few things out of many) that the minds were wholly without number and without name, and that all rational beings were one by identity of substance and operation, and of power, with God the Word through union and knowledge. These minds, however, when each according to its capacity had become sated with divine love and contemplation, through their change for the worse put on either grosser or finer bodies and received names, and hence the heavenly and ministering powers came into being. Indeed, [they say that] the sun, and the moon, and the stars too, as being themselves also in the unity of rational beings, began to be what they are through a change made for the worse. And those rational beings in whom the love of God grew colder are called psychai, that is, souls, and are sent into grosser bodies, such as ours are. And those which came to the extreme of perversity are inserted into cold and dark bodies, and become and are called demons; and accordingly from the angelic state comes the psychic, and from the psychic the demonic and the human. But only one mind out of the whole unity of rational beings remained undisturbed and unmoved from divine love and contemplation, and that this was Christ the King, God and man. They also assert that bodies will perish utterly, the Lord himself first, and then all the rest, casting off their bodies; and that all, returning again to the truth itself, become minds according to the being that they had before; and that evidently even the devil himself is to be restored, and the rest of the demons, into that unity, and impious and wicked men together with divine and God-filled men and the heavenly powers; and that they are to be united with God in the same way as Christ, just as they were united before, and so that Christ differs in no way at all from the other rational beings, neither in substance, nor in knowledge, nor in power, nor in operation. For Pythagoras said that the principle of all things was the monad; and again Pythagoras and Plato, saying that there is a certain multitude of incorporeal souls, say also that if they fall into some sin they are sent down into bodies as punishment. Hence Plato called the body demas (that is, a bond) and sema (that is, a tomb), because the soul is as it were bound and buried in the body itself. Then, concerning the future judgement and the requital of souls, he says again: The soul of him who together with the pursuit of wisdom has defiled himself with love of boys and a shameful life will pay the penalty through three thousand-year cycles, and so, having recovered its wings after thousands of years, it is led out and departs; but the rest, when they have departed from this life, some, carried beneath the earth to the place of judgement, will pay the penalty and at the same time give account; others, raised by judgement to a certain heavenly place, will enjoy happiness according to the merits of their life. It is easy, however, to see the absurdity of this opinion. For who taught him these thousand-year revolutions of years, and that after the course of a thousand years each soul arrives at its own place? And what he inserts among these things would not be fitting to be said even by shameless men, however lustful, let alone by such and so great a philosopher: for he joined those who led a life full of purity to the very end with the intemperate and the lovers of boys, and said that both enjoy the same goods. Pythagoras, then, and Plato, and Plotinus, and the others of their followers, who with one consent confess that souls are immortal, assert that they are prior to bodies, and that there is a certain multitude of souls, and that those which sin are sent down into bodies, as I have said, and that the souls of the lazy go off into asses, those of the rapacious into wolves, those of the deceitful into foxes, those given to the love of women into horses. But the Church, assenting to the divine Scriptures, affirms that the soul was created together with the body, not one before the other, as it seemed to the senseless Origen. On account of these abominable and pernicious opinions, then, or rather trifles, we exhort you, most holy Fathers, gathered together in one, to read carefully the exposition set out below, and to condemn each of its chapters, and to anathematise, together with Origen, all who think the same, or will think so to the end.
Confession of the right faith by the emperor Justinian against the Three Chapters.

In the name of God the Father, and of his Only-begotten Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and of the Holy Spirit. The Emperor Caesar, lover of Christ, Justinian, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, renowned, victor, triumphant, ever venerable, Augustus, to the whole assembly of the catholic and apostolic Church.

Knowing that nothing else can so appease the merciful God as that all Christians should think one and the same thing in the right and spotless faith, and that there should be no dissensions in the holy Church of God, we have thought it necessary, removing every occasion from those who are scandalised or who give scandal, to make manifest by the present edict the confession of the right faith which is preached in the holy Church of God: so that both those who confess the right faith may keep it firmly, and those who contend against it, learning the truth, may hasten to unite themselves to the holy Church of God.

We confess, then, that we believe in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, a consubstantial Trinity, one deity, or nature and substance and power and authority, adoring [it] in three hypostases or persons, in which we were baptised, in which we believe, in which we have made confession, separating the properties but uniting the deity. For we adore unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, which has a wonderful both division and union: unity according to the principle of substance or deity, and Trinity according to the properties, or hypostases, or persons. For it is divided without division (so to speak) and is joined dividedly. For the deity is one in three, and the three in which the deity is are one: or (to speak more precisely) the three themselves are the deity, which three are God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, when each person is understood alone, the mind separating things inseparable; and the three are one God, when they are understood together on account of the same power and the same nature: since one must both confess one God and proclaim three hypostases, or three persons, and each with its own property. And confessing the unity, we do not make a confusion according to Sabellius, who says that the Trinity is one person with three names, the same being Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit; nor, dividing the properties, do we estrange the Son and the Holy Spirit from the substance of God the Father, according to the madness of Arius, cutting the deity into three different natures. There is, then, one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.

We confess that this same Only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, born of the Father before the ages and without time, not made, in the last days for us and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, and was born of her; who is the Lord Jesus Christ, one of the holy Trinity, consubstantial with God the Father according to deity, and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, passible in the flesh, the same impassible in deity. For it is not some other besides God the Word who underwent suffering and death: but the impassible and everlasting God the Word himself, deigning to undergo the birth of human flesh, fulfilled all things. Therefore we do not acknowledge one God the Word who worked miracles and another Christ who suffered: but we confess one and the same our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, and that the miracles and the sufferings, which he willingly endured in the flesh, are of one and the same. For it was not some man who gave himself for us, but God the Word himself gave his own body for us, so that our faith and hope might not be in a man, but that we might have our faith in God the Word himself. And so, confessing him God, we do not deny that he is also man; and calling him man, we do not deny that he is also God. For if he were God only, how did he suffer? How was he crucified and how did he die? For these things are alien to God. But if [he were] man only, how did he conquer through suffering, how did he save? How did he give life? For these things were above the nature of man. But now the same one both suffers and saves, and conquers through suffering, the same one God, the same man, both as one, both as alone. Hence, saying that one Christ is composed from both natures, that is from deity and humanity, we do not introduce confusion into the union. And acknowledging in both natures, that is in divinity and humanity, one our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, we do not bring division into parts, or cutting, upon his one hypostasis; but we signify the difference of the natures from which he is composed, not destroyed on account of the union, since each nature is in him. For when we speak of composition, it is necessary to confess both that the parts are in the whole and that the whole is recognised in the parts. For neither was the divine nature changed into the human, nor was the human nature turned into the divine. Rather it is understood that, each remaining in the property and principle of its own nature, a union was made according to hypostasis. And union according to hypostasis signifies that God the Word, that is one hypostasis of the three hypostases of the deity, was not united to a man formed beforehand, but in the womb of the holy Virgin created for himself from her, in his own hypostasis, flesh animated with a rational and intellectual soul, which is human nature. Teaching us this union according to hypostasis of God the Word with the flesh, the divine Apostle too says: Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2). For by saying, Who, being in the form of God, he showed that the hypostasis of the Word is in the nature of God; and by saying, He took the form of a servant, he signified that God the Word was united to the nature of man, and not to a hypostasis or person. For he did not say that he took one who was in the form of a servant, lest he should show that God the Word was united to a man formed beforehand, as the impious Theodore and Nestorius blasphemed, speaking of a union of affection. But we, following the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, confess that God the Word was made flesh, which is to unite human nature to himself according to hypostasis: and therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is one, having in himself the perfection of the divine nature and the perfection of human nature. And he is the Only-begotten Word, as born of God the Father, and also the firstborn among many brothers, the same one when he was made man (for the Son of God was made son of man); and remaining what he was, he did not change what he was made. Hence we confess also two births of the same Only-begotten God the Word: the one before the ages from the Father, incorporeally; the other in the last days, of the same one incarnate and born of the holy, glorious Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. For he who shone forth from the Father beyond understanding arose from a mother beyond reason. And though he was true God, he truly became man. Therefore we confess the holy, glorious and ever-virgin Mary properly and truly Mother of God: not because God the Word took his beginning from her, but because in the last days the Only-begotten God the Word, who was before the ages, being incarnate from her, became man unchangeably; and though invisible in what is his, he became visible in what is ours; and though he was impassible God, he did not disdain to be a passible man; and, immortal, to be subject to the laws of death. This one, who was born in Bethlehem of the seed of David according to the flesh, and was made like men, and was crucified for men under Pontius Pilate, the holy apostles proclaimed to be himself God, himself man; himself Son of God, himself son of man; himself from heaven, himself from earth; himself impassible, himself passible. For God the Word, who was born from above of the Father ineffably, indescribably, incomprehensibly, eternally, is himself born in time below of the Virgin Mary, so that those who were first born below might be born a second time from above, that is of God. He then has only a mother on earth, and we have only a father in heaven. For having taken the mortal father of men, Adam, he gave men his own immortal Father, according to what is said: He gave them power to become sons of God (John 1). Hence also the Son of God tastes death according to the flesh, on account of his fleshly father, so that the sons of man might become partakers of his life, on account of his Father according to the spirit, God. He, then, is Son of God by nature, and we by grace; and again he, by dispensation and for our sake, was son of Adam, while we are sons of Adam by nature. For God is his Father by nature, but ours by grace. And he was God to him by dispensation, in that he was made man; but to us he is by nature Lord and God. And therefore God the Word, who is Son of God the Father, united to flesh, was made flesh, so that men united to the spirit might become one spirit. He, then, the true Son of God, put on all of us, so that we all might put on the one God. And even after the incarnation the Only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, composed of both natures, is one of the holy Trinity. And we confess Christ composite, following the teaching of the holy Fathers. For in the mystery of Christ the union by composition rejects confusion and division, and preserves the property of each nature, while it shows one hypostasis or person of God the Word even with the flesh; and he is one and the same perfect in deity and perfect in humanity, to be recognised not as in two hypostases or persons, but in the divine and human nature, so that he is one in both, perfect God and perfect man; the same Lord Jesus Christ, one of the holy Trinity, to be glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity did not receive the addition of a fourth person even when God the Word, one of the holy Trinity, was incarnate. This good tradition, then, which we received from the holy Fathers, we keep; in it we live and conduct ourselves, and, departing from this life, we pray to have it with us: which is the confession in the Father and in Christ the Son of the living God, and in the Holy Spirit.

Confessing these things in this way, and accepting, besides the other teachings of Saint Cyril on the right faith, also what he said, "one nature of God the Word incarnate," we confess that from the divine nature and the human one Christ was made, and not in one nature, as some, misunderstanding the phrase, try to say. Hence the Father himself, whenever he spoke of one nature of the Word incarnate, used the name "nature" here for "hypostasis." And in the books in which he used this phrase, he often added in what follows both "Son" and "Word" or "Only-begotten," which signify not a nature but a hypostasis or person. The hypostasis of the Word, then, being incarnate, produced not one nature but one composite Christ, the same being God and man. But for those who confess Christ as God and man to speak of one nature or substance of him is impious. For it is impossible that our Lord Jesus Christ should, according to one and the same nature or substance, be both before the ages and in time, or impassible and passible: which we rightly confess in his one hypostasis or person. From the very words of the same Saint Cyril we shall show his clear teaching on the phrase mentioned. For in the first letter to Succensus, having said "one nature of God the Word incarnate," he at once added: "Therefore, as far as concerns the understanding, and seeing only with the eyes of the soul the way in which the Only-begotten was incarnate, we say that two natures were united, but one Son and Christ and Lord, the Word of God the Father incarnate and made man." By these words the Father, wishing to make plain the manner of the incarnation, and keeping the union undivided and unconfused, both pointed out the number of the natures which came together and proclaimed one Christ, and not one nature of the deity and the flesh. And in the second letter to the same Succensus, teaching similar things, he writes thus: "For if, saying one nature of the Word, we had kept silent, not adding 'incarnate', but as it were setting the dispensation outside, there would perhaps have been for them even a plausible ground, in their fabrications, to ask: where is the perfection in humanity, or how does our human substance subsist? But since both the perfection in humanity and the indication of our substance have been brought in by saying 'incarnate', let them cease leaning on a staff of reed. For one who threw out the dispensation and denied the incarnation would justly have to be accused of taking from the Son his perfect humanity. But if (as I said) by saying that he was incarnate there is a clear and indubitable confession that he was made man, nothing now prevents [us from] understanding that, since Christ is one and the only Son, the same is God and man, perfect in deity as also perfect in humanity. And most rightly and very prudently your perfection sets out the account of the saving passion, affirming not that the Only-begotten Son of God himself, in so far as he is understood to be and is God, suffered in his own nature the things of the body, but rather that he suffered in the earthly nature. For both must of necessity be preserved for the one and true Son: both not to suffer according to the deity, and that the same be said to have suffered according to the humanity; for his flesh suffered." And in the thirteenth chapter of the Scholia the same Saint Cyril, likewise rejecting both those who introduce two sons and those who speak of one nature of the deity and the flesh of Christ, writes thus: "The one Lord Jesus Christ is not to be divided into a man separately and into God separately; but we speak of one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, knowing the difference of the natures and keeping them unconfused with one another." If, then (as Saint Cyril teaches us), our Lord Jesus Christ is one, perfect in deity and the same perfect in humanity, and the divine nature did not suffer but the earthly, and he knows both the difference of the natures and that they are kept unconfused with one another in one hypostasis: it is certain that the Father says the same one is recognised in the divine nature and in the human, and that both natures are in him, from which he is also composed. And let no one be so mad as to think that those think rightly who say that there is one nature or substance of the flesh and the deity of Christ, the same both divine and earthly, passible and impassible.

But since some also try in another way to show that there is one nature of the deity and humanity of Christ, putting forward the example of man and saying that, just as man, consisting of different natures, soul and body, is called one nature, so too, speaking of Christ from two natures, deity and humanity, we ought to speak of his one nature: this we shall say to them, that man, although he consists of different things, that is, soul and body, is nevertheless called one nature because it is predicated in common of all the hypostases or persons which are referred to the same species. For although each hypostasis or person, such as Peter and Paul, is separated from the other by properties, yet they are not divided in nature: for both are men; and again, neither the soul without the body nor the body without the soul is a man, but [man] was created from soul and body, out of what he was not into what he is. And each creature, although it consists of different things, is nevertheless said to have that one nature according to which it was created by God. But Christ is not so: for he does not signify one nature or substance which is predicated in common of very many hypostases or persons, as "man" is. For if this were so, many christs would be found, of whom the community of one nature would be predicated; which it is impious even to say. Nor was Christ created from the beginning out of deity and humanity, as man out of soul and body, so that this should be the nature of Christ: but since the Word was God before the ages, and was of the same nature or substance as the Father, and the creator of all things, in the last days, uniting to himself the nature of man according to hypostasis, he became man while remaining God.

Christ, then, is one hypostasis or person, and has in himself the perfection of the divine and uncreatable nature and the perfection of the human and creatable nature. How then is it possible to speak of one nature or substance in him in whom two natures are recognised, uncreatable and creatable? For although Christ is one hypostasis or person, yet the same is consubstantial with God the Father and consubstantial with us, not however according to one and the same nature or substance. But if Christ were one nature or substance, either he is without flesh and consubstantial only with God the Father [and the Spirit, Greek], since the substance or nature of the deity is one; or, being a mere man, he is consubstantial only with us, since the nature of humanity is one; or both natures, being changed, produced another nature besides those which came together, and according to them Christ neither remained God nor became man, and therefore the same is consubstantial neither with the Father nor with us. To think thus is full of every impiety. And we say these things not unaware that some of the holy Fathers too used the example of man in the mystery of Christ: but they did so to show that, just as man is made one from soul and body, and not two men, so too Christ, composed of deity and humanity, is one, not to be divided into two christs or two sons. These people, however, use the example of man in order to introduce one nature or substance of the deity and humanity of Christ: which we have shown to be foreign to piety. But when they are convicted by these arguments of fabricating for themselves, contrary to the right teaching of the Fathers, one nature or substance of the deity and the flesh, they pass to other things, saying that one ought not to speak of a number of natures in Christ, since number introduces division. Let them know, then, that number, when it is spoken of in different persons or hypostases, involves a division of the things themselves into parts, as in two or even more men; but when [it is spoken of] in things united, then [it divides] in word alone [in reason alone] and in understanding, but not by a division of the things themselves, as in the one hypostasis of a man constituted from soul and body. For here too two natures are understood, one of the soul and the other of the body: and yet he is not on this account divided into two men, but we know that he is one man, and his hypostasis one. In the mystery of Christ, then, once the union has been made, although the things united are understood to be different, yet the things from which our Lord Jesus Christ is composed are not separated from one another in reality itself and by parts; but considering the difference and wishing to signify it, we take up number and say that there are two natures in Christ: and not for that reason is the one Christ divided into two christs or two sons. And Saint Gregory the Theologian bears witness to our words, writing thus in the first book to Cledonius: "If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, and a second from the mother, but not one and the same, let him fall from the adoption which is promised to those who believe rightly. For the natures are two, God [and] man, as also soul and body; but not two sons, nor two gods. For neither are these two men, although Paul so named (1 Cor. 4) what is within a man and what is outside: and, to speak briefly, the things from which the Saviour is are one thing and another, since the invisible and the visible are not the same, nor that which is without time and that which is under time: but not one person and another: far from it."

See, by these words Saint Gregory clearly teaches that in the mystery of Christ the one who speaks of number in the persons is condemned as impious, while the one who admits number in the natures from which the one Christ is composed confesses rightly, since by this he signifies the difference of the natures which came together, but in no way makes a division by parts. For just as the nature of the soul is one thing and that of the body another, and yet by composition one man is made, and not two men; so too in Christ, although two natures are understood, one of deity and the other of humanity, yet not on this account are two christs or two sons introduced. Therefore those who refuse to speak, in the way described, of the number of the natures that are in Christ are plainly denying the difference of the natures and introducing confusion into the dispensation. But if they confess the difference, it is altogether necessary, in order to signify it, also to speak of the number of the natures which came together without confusion into one hypostasis. For where difference is preserved, there number in every way follows as well. To confirm what we have said, using the testimony of the holy Fathers, we shall show that they say that in [the mystery of Christ, Greek] our one Lord Jesus Christ the accounts are indeed divided according to the difference of the natures of deity and humanity from which he is also composed, and that they take up number in this, yet do not make a division of the natures in reality itself and by parts into two hypostases or persons.

For Saint Cyril, in his interpretation of Leviticus (Lev. 14), says thus: "In these things again consider openly the whole mystery of our Saviour, and the cleansing that comes about through holy baptism. For he commands two little birds to be taken, living and clean, so that you may understand by the winged creatures the heavenly man who is at the same time God, to be divided into two natures, so far as concerns the account proper to each. For God the Word, since he is from God the Father, shone forth in the flesh, since it is from a woman; yet he is not to be parted, for Christ is one, and from both." And again the same Saint Cyril, in the second letter to Succensus, says thus: "But they did not know that things which are usually divided by the understanding alone will not necessarily also be separated from one another, altogether and individually, into an otherness that is by parts." And Saint Basil too, in the fourth book against Eunomius, interpreting this text, The Lord created me, and before all the hills he begot me (Prov. 9), writes thus: "What he says, created, is to be understood of him who received the form of a servant. But in all these things we do not speak of two, God separately and man separately, for he was one: but [we speak so] by the understanding, considering the nature of each." And Saint Gregory the Theologian also, in the second book on the Son, teaching us how in our Lord Jesus Christ we ought to distinguish by the understanding the natures that are in him, writes thus: "When the natures are distinguished by the understanding, the names too are divided along with them. Hear Paul saying: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory (Eph. 1): God of Christ, but Father of glory. For although both are one, yet [they are one] not by nature but by coming together." And Saint Gregory of Nyssa [bishop of Nyssa], in the fourth book against Eunomius, teaching us the same things, writes thus: "And lest anyone should apply the suffering of the cross to the incorruptible nature, he corrects such an error more clearly by other words, naming him the mediator of God and men (1 Tim. 2), and naming him both man and God: so that, since two things are said of one, what is fitting may be understood regarding each, impassibility regarding the deity, and the dispensation of suffering regarding the humanity. So, since the understanding divides what has been united through mercy but is distinguished by reason, when he proclaims what is set above and surpasses all sense, he uses loftier names, calling him God over all, and great God, and power of God, and wisdom (Rom. 9; Titus 2; 1 Cor. 1), and such things; but when in words he signifies the experience of sufferings, necessarily accepted on account of our weakness, naming each from what is ours he calls him man, not by the word making the one signified common to the other nature, but so that piety may be preserved regarding each."

These things having been thus demonstrated through the teaching of the holy Fathers, let those cease who make the number of the natures that are in Christ the occasion of their error, and who, denying their difference [by denying the difference on this account, Greek] through refusing number, try to introduce confusion. For how is number not necessary, when the Fathers used it to signify the difference of the natures that were united into one hypostasis, and not for their division by parts? It is therefore demonstrated on every side that it is impious to speak of one nature or substance of the deity and the flesh of Christ; and we say this too, that it is not possible, in the way that we speak of one hypostasis of the deity and humanity of Christ, likewise to speak also of one nature of Christ: since nature and hypostasis are not the same. For all the holy Fathers teach us with one voice that nature or substance and form is one thing, and hypostasis or person another; and that nature or substance and form signifies what is common, while hypostasis or person signifies what is particular. But if some should say that, just as one composite hypostasis of Christ is spoken of, so one ought also to speak of one composite nature: we shall show that this too is foreign to piety. For in speaking of one nature or substance of the deity, we confess [glorify, Greek] three hypostases of it, recognising in each hypostasis the same nature or substance. And we rightly say that, of the three hypostases, the one hypostasis of the Word was composed with flesh. For no one in the catholic Church has ever dared to say that, as there are three hypostases, so there are also three natures of the holy Trinity, so that it would be possible to say that one nature out of three natures was composed with flesh. For Arius alone dared to speak of three natures in the holy Trinity, and he was condemned as a blasphemer. Therefore, according to right reason, we speak of a union of two natures and of one hypostasis: since the Son of God, though he was in hypostasis other than the Father, yet having the same nature as the Father, formed for himself in his own hypostasis flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul; which signifies that God the Word was united to human nature, and not to the hypostasis or person of some individual. God the Word, then, also incarnate, is to be recognised as one hypostasis in each nature: in the divine, in which he was, as it is said, Who, being in the form of God (Phil. 2); and in the human, according as he was made in the likeness of men (ibid.). And so one would more rightly [piously, Greek] speak of one composite hypostasis of God the Word than of one composite nature: since, when nature is spoken of by itself absolutely, with no particular person of anyone added to it, it signifies something indeterminate and not subsisting; and what is indeterminate cannot be composed with anything. But if anyone, even after such arguments, looking only to contention, tries to object, saying that according to the account given of nature the human nature of Christ too must have its own proper hypostasis or person: such a one is manifestly saying that God the Word was united to a man who already subsisted, and that the union came about by affection. For two hypostases or persons cannot be united according to hypostasis. He who says these things, then, hastening to empty the power of God by words of human wisdom, does not know the great mystery of piety, which is believed with the heart unto righteousness, and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. For the human nature of Christ is never spoken of by itself absolutely, nor did it have its own hypostasis or person: but in the hypostasis of God the Word the human nature had the beginning [received the beginning of existence, Greek] of its being; whence we confess that God the Word himself became man unchangeably, and did not come into some man; and that the birth from the virgin belongs to the same God the Word incarnate, and for this reason that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God. Therefore both before the incarnation of God the Word and after his incarnation we speak of three hypostases, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity did not receive the addition of a fourth hypostasis or person. From all these things, therefore, those who say that there were two natures before the union are convicted of saying that the man was formed [subsisted] beforehand and was thus united to God the Word, according to the madness of the impious Theodore and Nestorius. And those who say that after the union one ought to speak not of two natures in Christ but of one introduce confusion and phantasm, according to the impious Apollinarius and Eutyches. These men say such things. But the holy Fathers, considering after the incarnation of God the Word the things from which Christ is, and that the natures remained unconfused, most rightly said that there are two natures in Christ, the divine and the human. For neither were there two natures of the Lord before the incarnation, nor after the incarnation did the two natures become one, although they are recognised in one hypostasis.

Taught these things both from the divine Scriptures and from the teaching of the Fathers, we have rightly written them to refute those who confuse and divide the mystery of the divine dispensation; and it is not by declaring the things from which Christ is, and in which he is recognised, that we bring confusion or division into the divine dispensation. Therefore, setting forth the glorification and the account of the union, we confess and worship one Christ and Son and Lord, the Word of God incarnate and made man, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Confessing these things thus with the universal Church of God, we wish all Christians to know that, as we have one God and Lord, so we have also one faith. For there is one definition of faith: to confess and rightly glorify the Father, and Christ the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit. This confession we preserve, in which we were also baptised, given by our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ to his holy disciples and apostles, and preached by them in the whole world. And the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers gathered at Nicaea against Arius, after he had been condemned with his impiety, handed down this same confession, that is, the holy lesson and creed of faith, to the holy Church of God; and after them the hundred and fifty holy Fathers gathered at Constantinople against Macedonius, who fought against the Holy Spirit, and Magnus the Apollinarist, after these had been condemned with their perfidy, following in all things the same holy creed handed down by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, explained what concerns the deity of the Holy Spirit (Acts 5). Moreover, both the holy Fathers who earlier gathered at Ephesus against the impious Nestorius, and the holy Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, following in all things the aforesaid holy creed or lesson of faith, condemned the aforesaid heretics together with their impiety, and those who thought or think like them. And besides this they anathematised those who hand down another definition of faith, or creed, or lesson to those coming to holy baptism, or converted from any heresy whatever, other than that handed down (as has been said) by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and explained by the hundred and fifty holy Fathers. Since these things are so, we have seen fit also to append chapters, in which are contained both a brief confession of the right faith and the condemnation of the heretics.

1. If anyone does not confess the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, a consubstantial Trinity, one deity or nature and substance, and one power and authority, to be worshipped in three hypostases or persons, let such a one be anathema.

2. If anyone does not confess that he who was born of the Father before the ages and without time, God the Word, in the last days came down from heaven and was made flesh of the holy, glorious Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and, having become man, was born of her, and that for this reason there are two births of the same God the Word, [namely the eternal one and] the one in the last days according to the flesh, let such a one be anathema.

3. If anyone says that God the Word who worked miracles is one, and the Christ who suffered is another, or says that God the Word was with Christ as he was born of a woman, or was in him as one in another, and not that our Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word made flesh and become man, is one and the same, and that the miracles and the sufferings which he willingly endured in the flesh belong to this same one, let such a one be anathema.

4. If anyone says that the union of God the Word with the man came about according to grace, or according to operation, or according to dignity, or according to equality of honour, or according to authority, or relation, or affection, or power, or according to homonymy, by which the Nestorians, both calling God the Word Christ and naming the man separately Christ, speak of one Christ by the name alone; or if anyone says that the union came about through good will, as the heretic Theodore says in these very words, as though the man pleased God the Word because he thought well of him, and does not confess the union according to hypostasis of God the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, and therefore that his one hypostasis is composite, let such a one be anathema.

5. If anyone calls the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary Mother of God by relation or in an improper sense, or mother of a man, or *Christotokos* [mother of Christ], as though Christ were not God, and does not confess her to be properly and truly Mother of God, because he who was born of the Father before the ages, God the Word, in the last days was made flesh and born of her, let such a one be anathema.
6. If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified in the flesh, is true God, and Lord of glory, and one of the holy Trinity, let such a one be anathema.

7. If anyone, saying "in two natures", does not confess one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word made flesh, as in deity and humanity, nor [uses it] to signify the difference of the natures from which he is composed, but takes such an expression in the mystery of Christ for a division into parts, as though each nature had separately its own hypostasis, as Theodore and Nestorius blasphemed, let such a one be anathema.

8. If anyone, confessing the number of the natures in the one Lord Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word made flesh, does not take in thought the difference of those from which he is also composed, as a difference not abolished by the union, but uses the number for a division into parts, let such a one be anathema.

9. If anyone, saying "one nature of God the Word incarnate", does not understand this to mean that from the divine nature and the human one Christ was made, consubstantial with the Father according to the deity, and the same one consubstantial with us according to the humanity, but that one nature or substance of the deity and the flesh of Christ came about, according to the perfidy of Apollinarius and Eutyches, let such a one be anathema.
10. For the universal Church of God equally rejects and condemns both those who cut or divide into parts and those who confound the mystery of Christ's divine dispensation.
If anyone does not anathematise Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who have thought or think like them, let such a one be anathema.

11. If anyone defends Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said that God the Word is one, and Christ another, who suffered troubles from the passions of the soul and the desires of the flesh, and was improved by progress in works, and was baptised in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and through baptism received the grace of the Holy Spirit and earned adoption as son, and like an imperial image is worshipped [was worshipped] in the person of God the Word, and after the resurrection became unchangeable in his thoughts and altogether sinless; and who again said that the union of God the Word with Christ came about such as the Apostle spoke of concerning husband and wife: "The two shall be in one flesh" (Eph. 5); and who, besides his other countless blasphemies, dared to say that when after the resurrection the Lord breathed on his disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20), he did not give them the Holy Spirit, but only breathed on them figuratively; and also he said that the confession which Thomas made when he had touched the hands and side of the Lord after the resurrection, saying, "My Lord and my God" (ibid.), was not said by Thomas of Christ (for Theodore did not say that Christ is God), but that Thomas, astonished at the miracle of the resurrection, glorified God who raised Christ; and, what is worse, in the commentary which Theodore wrote on the Acts of the Apostles he likened Christ to Plato, and Mani, and Epicurus, and Marcion, saying that just as each of them, from the doctrine he devised, caused his disciples to be called Platonists, and Manichaeans, and Epicureans, and Marcionites, in like manner, when Christ had devised a doctrine, [people] were called Christians from him. If anyone therefore defends this Theodore, who uttered such blasphemies, and does not anathematise him and his writings, and those who have thought or think like him, let such a one be anathema.

12. If anyone defends the writings of Theodoret which he set out for the heretic Nestorius against the right faith, and the first holy synod of Ephesus, and Saint Cyril and his twelve chapters, in which wicked writings this Theodoret speaks of a union by affection of God the Word with a certain man, concerning whom he said blasphemously that Thomas touched him who rose and worshipped him who raised [him]; and on this account he calls impious the teachers of the Church who confess the union according to hypostasis of God the Word with the flesh; and besides this he denies that the holy and glorious ever-virgin Mary is Mother of God. If anyone therefore defends the said writings of Theodoret and does not anathematise them, let such a one be anathema. For because of such blasphemies he was cast out of the episcopate, and afterwards at the holy council of Chalcedon he was compelled to do everything contrary to his said writings and to confess the right faith.

13. If anyone defends the impious letter which Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian, a heretic, which denies that God the Word became man, and says that it was not God the Word made flesh of the virgin who was born, but that a mere man was born of her, whom it calls a temple, so that God the Word is one and the man another; and which besides this insults the first synod of Ephesus, [saying] that Nestorius was condemned by it without inquiry and examination, and calls Saint Cyril a heretic, and calls his twelve chapters impious, while it praises and defends Nestorius and Theodore with their impious writings. If anyone therefore, as has been said, upholds this same letter, or says that it or a part of it is right, and does not anathematise it, let him be anathema. Now although such an impious letter has justly been anathematised because of the blasphemies inserted in it, the followers of the impious Theodore and Nestorius try to say that it was received by the holy council of Chalcedon. They say this, slandering the holy synod of Chalcedon, and hastening in its name to free from due condemnation Theodore and Nestorius and the impious letter, which Ibas, though often accused over it, did not dare to call his own because of the blasphemies inserted in it. And we shall show this from what was variously set in motion concerning this case. For in the proceedings before Photius and Eustathius [by Photius and Eustathius] at Tyre, when the said Ibas was accused of insults against Saint Cyril, he plainly confessed that after the union of the Easterners which was made with Cyril of holy memory he had said nothing insulting about him. But the letter, full of the said blasphemies for which Ibas was accused, and containing many insults against Saint Cyril, is shown to have been written after the union made with the Easterners, from which it is demonstrated that Ibas denied it. Hence the said Photius and Eustathius, satisfying the accusers, decreed in writing that the said Ibas should do everything contrary to the letter, as the judgement given by them on this matter indicates. But since Ibas did not carry out what they had judged, he was cast out of the episcopate because of the blasphemies of the said letter, and Nonnus was ordained in his place, who also sat in the holy council of Chalcedon. Accused, then, on the same matters at Chalcedon also, the said Ibas, after the reading of the impious letter, did not dare to confess it to be his, but at once added in these very words that he was a stranger to the things charged against him. Hence the holy synod, since Ibas's denial made concerning the impious letter did not satisfy it, compelled him to do the contrary of it, that is, to confess the right faith rejected in it, and to receive the first holy synod of Ephesus, and to acknowledge as Father and teacher Saint Cyril, who are insulted in that impious letter, and to anathematise Nestorius and his impious doctrine, which the impious letter also defends and praises. If, then, Ibas himself, often accused because of the impious letter, did not dare to call it his own, and moreover the holy council of Chalcedon compelled him to do everything contrary to it, how could the same holy synod receive the said letter and subject itself to the condemnation of the impiety contained in it, from which it hastened to free Ibas? And since the heretics, passing over all the blasphemies of the letter, bring forward from it only what the writer of the letter said to deceive the simpler sort, that is, two natures, one power, one person, we shall show that even in this he mixed in his own impiety. For of whom could he speak of two natures and one person, who denies that God the Word was made flesh of the holy and glorious Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary and was born of her? Rather it is certain that he attributes to each nature its own person, as Theodore and Nestorius set out blasphemously in their books, whom the writer of the letter defends along with their impiety. For they, openly speaking of two persons, of God the Word and of Christ, whom they call a mere man, say that one person appears through a conjunction by affection and through the same dignity and honour; and the writer of the letter, speaking also of one power or might of the two natures, is clearly following the said heretics in this too, Theodore saying in various books impiously set out on the incarnation, and Nestorius in many writings, and especially in the letter written to Alexander of Hierapolis, a heretic, that there is one authority of the two natures, and one power or might, and one person [according to one] through dignity and the same honour: from which it is shown that he who wrote the letter, following their perfidy, used the word "natures" for "persons". For one authority, and one power or might, and one dignity and the same honour are said not of different natures but of different persons of the same substance, which we confess in the holy Trinity. Hence the holy Fathers also anathematised those who say that God the Word was united to Christ through authority, or power or might, or dignity, or equality of honour, whom the followers of Theodore and Nestorius call a mere man, and do not confess that the union came about according to hypostasis of God the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul.

And these things would indeed have been enough to convict of impiety those who champion the wicked letter. Yet at its end, too, the writer of that letter shows his perfidy, by saying that one must believe in the temple and in him who dwells in the temple, by which he openly introduces two persons. This impiety too the writer of the letter learned from Theodore and Nestorius. But the Catholic Church, condemning such perfidy, teaches us to confess and believe not in the temple and in him who dwells in the temple, but in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made man. It is no wonder that the writer of that impious letter used the word "natures". For heretics, in order to deceive the simpler, are accustomed to use words that are piously spoken by the orthodox, but to turn their right understanding and explanation to their own impiety. The same words, when they are well explained and understood, are [sometimes] pious; but when they are badly understood and uttered by heretics, they carry impiety. Thus Nestorius spoke of two natures and one person, but did not confess their union according to hypostasis; and so the first synod of Ephesus, whose authors were Celestine and Cyril of holy memory, did not receive him, but condemned him. But we, following the teaching of the holy Fathers in all things, have shown more plainly above both the union of the two natures from which our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the holy Trinity, God the Word incarnate, is composed, and that their difference was not abolished on account of the union. What we have said already would indeed have been enough to satisfy those who do not wish to quarrel. But since those who have once turned aside to impiety try to put forward other arguments as well, we must also show that these pretexts of theirs are empty. For they say that the impious letter ought not to be censured, because it is found in a number of codices. But if anyone accepts this, as their madness would have it, then Nestorius and Eutyches must also be accepted, since a great deal about them too is contained in the records of what was done at the synod. But no wise man will pay attention to what they say. For whatever is brought forward concerning heretics at synods and becomes part of the records is inserted not for their acquittal, but for the greater condemnation of them and of those who think as they do. And although copies of the impious letter that are circulated have been inserted in some codices, as has been said, they are nowhere found in the authentic ones to which the most holy bishops subscribed. Those who search out the truth should also bear in mind that at councils certain things may perhaps be said by particular persons gathered there, out of favour, or out of opposition, or out of ignorance. But no one pays attention to what is said by some individuals in part, but only to what is defined by all with common consent. For if anyone wished, as they do, to attend to contradictions of this kind, every synod would be found destroying itself. For these reasons, then, if they rightly accepted the holy council, they ought not to have attached such blasphemies to it, but to have followed the teachers of the Catholic Church, and above all Saint Athanasius, who was bishop of Alexandria and undertook very many and great labours for the right faith of Christians against every heresy, and above all against the most impious Arians. For when the Arians themselves, in order to deceive the people, joined to their error Dionysius, who was bishop of Alexandria many years before Athanasius, and said that this Dionysius too thought as they did, Athanasius, the great teacher of the Church, showed in many ways in his writings that Dionysius had preached the right faith from the beginning and had in no way shared the Arian impiety. But these men, who think heretical things, hasten to attach their impiety to this synod. What condemnation there is, and what curse hangs over those who sin against the Fathers, divine Scripture also teaches us. For if Ham the son of Noah (Gen. 9), when he had seen his father naked, because he did not cover his father's bodily nakedness, but went out and told his brothers of it, and they covered it with a garment, came under a curse, both Ham himself and those born of him, while those who covered it earned a great blessing: how much more are these men worthy of a greater and fuller condemnation, who hasten, through the impiety of the letter and of Theodore, to attach to the holy synod a disgrace that in no way belongs to it. But not for that reason will the impious letter, or those who defend it, escape the condemnation of their impiety; nor will Theodore, who surpasses pagans and Jews and all heretics in impiety. For it was not enough for the impious Theodore, besides his other blasphemies, to interpret the creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers wrongly to suit his error; but, despising it, he even set out another creed full of every impiety, in which he dared to anathematise those who think or teach otherwise, so that, as far as his madness was concerned, all the holy apostles and Fathers would be condemned. This impious creed of Theodore was both brought forward at the first synod of Ephesus and read out at that of Chalcedon, and was condemned by both synods, together with its author and those who accept it.

Since some who plead for Theodore, when his impious writings are brought forward, pretend indeed to say that they are impious because of the blasphemy contained in them, yet refuse to anathematise the man himself who spewed out such impiety, we wonder at their madness, that they act contrary to divine Scripture, which plainly says that equally hateful to God are the impious man and his impiety (Wisd. 14). For the deed will be punished with its doer. And if he who acts impiously is as hateful to God as the impiety, then surely such a man is separated from God, and is justly subjected to anathema. For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, as the judgement concerning anathema signifies in the Old and New Testament. And that the Lord too says that those who do not abide in the word of his truth are separated from the Church, he declares in the Gospel according to John, addressing the Jews thus: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever" (John 8). And that what the Lord names the house divine Scripture calls the Church of the living God, the Apostle testifies in the First Letter to Timothy (ch. 3).

But if some say that Theodore ought not to be anathematised after death, let those who defend such a heretic know that every heretic who remains in his error to the end of his life is justly subjected to perpetual anathema even after death. And this has been done in the case of many heretics, both older and more recent, that is, Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, Mani, Eunomius and Bonosus. The same was done in the case of Theodore too, who was both accused in his lifetime and anathematised after death by the holy Fathers; and if the heretics who defend him will not believe them, let them believe the impious letter which they themselves defend. For although it praises Theodore, it nevertheless says plainly that he was anathematised in the Church by the holy Fathers, and that from then on a very great inquiry was made into his writings, as being full of impiety. The teachers of the Catholic Church did this at that time so that the simpler, reading his impious writings, should not turn aside from the right faith. And that the impious, even if they did not receive anathema in person during their lifetime, are nevertheless anathematised by the Catholic Church after death, is shown by the holy synods. For the synod of Nicaea anathematised, without naming them, those who follow the impious sect of Arius. And that which was assembled at Constantinople likewise condemned the impious heresy of Macedonius; yet the holy Church of God anathematises Arius and Macedonius by name even after death. And when they are convicted by many proofs that those who defend Theodore and his impiety act vainly and impiously, they take refuge in another empty pretext, saying that he ought not to be anathematised because he died in the communion of the Churches. But they ought to know that those die in the communion of the Churches who have kept to the end the common doctrine of piety which is preached in the universal Church. This man, however, remaining in his impiety until death, was cast out by the whole Church. And so the whole body of the Church of Mopsuestia, in which he is said to have been bishop, because of the blasphemies for which, as it found, he had been numbered by the holy Fathers with pagans and Jews and Sodomites, itself struck his name from the sacred diptychs of the Church, as the records drawn up on this matter in that city before the council of the bishops of that province show. We wonder, then, at the followers of Theodore, who defend him and his impiety as if it were their own, when the Church in which he was bishop cast him out long ago as a heretic. That the defenders of Theodore put forward such a pretext to their own condemnation may be learned also from the dreadful judgement passed on Judas. For he, having supposed that he was hidden from him who knows the secrets of men, shared in the sacraments with the apostles; but it profited him nothing that he shared in them with guile. And although after his death the disciples are named as twelve, as John the evangelist says, "But Thomas, who was called Didymus, one of the twelve, was not with them when Jesus came" (John 20), yet this does not free Judas from condemnation, or cause him to be counted among the apostles. Hence after the ascension of the Lord the apostles by their sentence condemned this Judas even after death, and brought in another in his place (Acts 1). And that they put forward an empty pretext in saying that dead heretics ought not to be anathematised, we shall show also from the very words of the Lord. For he names the impious, even while still living, dead, saying, "Let the dead bury their dead" (Matt. 8), just as he names the righteous, though already departed, living. For he says of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob that God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt. 22). If therefore, according to their words, dead heretics ought not to be anathematised, neither will living heretics be anathematised, whom the Lord calls dead because they are separated from him who said, "I am the life" (John 11 and 14); and so, according to them, heretics will be anathematised neither living nor dead; and in vain, according to them, does the apostolic teaching (Gal. 1) direct that those who teach anything beyond what we have received be anathematised; in vain did the holy synods condemn heretics; in vain did the other holy Fathers and teachers of the Church anathematise heretics. Let them also find fault with the prophet Jeremiah, who says, "Cursed is he who does the works of the Lord negligently" (Jer. 48); and with the prophet David, who says, "Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments" (Ps. 118); and, to put it briefly, with all divine Scripture, which in various places brings such condemnations upon the impious. But if those who do the works of God negligently and sin against his commandments are subjected to such condemnations, how much more justly was the impious Theodore, who uttered such blasphemies against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ himself, condemned and anathematised?

And these things indeed would have sufficed, on top of the proofs mentioned above and inserted in our other books, which we have put forward to show that heretics ought to be condemned even after death, to confound those who defend Theodore and to restrain them from such impiety. But since they contentiously persist in the same [views], we also say, what is more, that some of those who assembled at the holy synod of Nicaea and subscribed to the definition of faith, or creed, set out by it, because they afterwards appeared to hold contrary views, were anathematised, some while living and others after death, by Damasus of holy memory, pope of elder Rome, and by the universal synod of Sardica, as holy Athanasius testifies. And the holy synod of Chalcedon too condemned after death Domnus, who had been made bishop of Antioch, because he had merely dared to write that the twelve chapters of holy Cyril ought to be passed over in silence.

But since the heretical defenders of Theodore, failing in every argument and attempt, presume to say, to deceive the ignorant, that Cyril of holy memory praised him in some part of a letter, it is shown from many [passages] that their attempt does not agree with what was said by holy Cyril in his various books against the impious Theodore, in which, showing him to be more impious than all other heretics, and then not enduring his very many and very great blasphemies uttered against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, he cried out, saying thus: "Heaven was appalled at this, and shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord. O intolerable malice, O tongue speaking iniquity against God, and lifting up its horn on high!" And again: "Set, man, a door and a bolt on your tongue; stop lifting up your horn on high and speaking iniquity against God. How long will you insult the suffering Christ? Bear in mind what was written by the divine Paul: 'When you sin thus against the brethren and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ' (1 Cor. 8). And to say something also from the prophetic books: 'Sodom has been justified by you' (Ezek. 16); you have surpassed the verbosities of the pagans which they produced against Christ, reckoning the cross foolishness (1 Cor. 1); you have shown the crimes of Jewish arrogance to be nothing." Since, then, these things were said thus by holy Cyril for the condemnation of Theodore, even if someone grants that, according to their words, holy Cyril said something in favour of Theodore, not even this frees him from condemnation. For we find that many of the holy Fathers praised certain heretics, as holy Damasus and Athanasius and Basil [praised] Apollinarius, and holy Leo Eutyches; and yet, once their impiety was recognised, the heretics did not for that reason escape the condemnation and anathema which was afterwards pronounced against their person and their impiety. So great, moreover, is the fury of those defending Theodore that they presume to lie against Gregory the Theologian and John of Constantinople, saying that they sent letters full of praise to this same Theodore: which is false. For Gregory, when, after labouring for the truth in Constantinople and turning the peoples through his efforts from the Arian madness to the catholic faith, he returned to his homeland, wrote the letters which the heretics craftily bring forward not to Theodore of Mopsuestia but to Theodore, bishop of Tyana, which is the metropolis of Second Cappadocia. To the same province belong both the city of Nazianzus, of which this same Gregory of holy memory had been bishop, and the estate of Arianzus, where he was born. This the letters themselves plainly indicate, making mention of customs and assemblies, and of this same estate of Arianzus and other estates of the same province, and of a month named in the native tongue of the Cappadocians, and of Bosporius, a bishop placed under this same Theodore, who at that time was bishop of the city of Colonia in the same province, and of other bishops and chorepiscopi and monasteries which were under Theodore's jurisdiction, whose names are preserved the same to this day. What connection, moreover, did the Cappadocians have with Second Cilicia, whether then or now, since the government of those provinces was separate? And what bishops could the bishop of Mopsuestia have had under him, when he himself was placed under the metropolitan of Second Cilicia? John of Constantinople did indeed write a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia, yet full not of praises but of complaints and rebukes, since he had fallen away from the good way of life. For since he had practised the monastic life with him in one and the same monastery, he reminded him of the way of life led there; and to this Sozomen, Hesychius, Socrates and Theodoret bear witness, [the last of] whom composed many speeches and praises on behalf of Theodore. And if they bring forward testimonies of John of Antioch and of the Eastern council under him, made in favour of Theodore and his impiety, they must also accept those things which (as far as it lay with them) John and those who were with him did for the condemnation of holy Cyril and the rejection of the right faith, and also what they wrote while defending Nestorius and his perfidy for a long time. And this is shown from their various books and letters which they wrote to Theodosius of pious memory and to various others.

And these things are so. But that we may pass over nothing of precision, we thought it necessary to recall also what was written by Augustine of holy memory, the African bishop. For when some question was raised after the death of Caecilian concerning him, because he was said to have departed from ecclesiastical tradition, and for this reason certain people had separated from the catholic Church, this same holy Augustine writes to Boniface that some ought not on that account to separate themselves from the catholic Church: "For if the things charged against Caecilian were true, and it had been shown that he held anything contrary to the Church's established order, I would subject him to anathema even after death." And a canon of the holy African synod also laid down that bishops who leave their property to a heretic, by will or intestate, ought to be anathematised even after death. Besides all this, who does not know what was done in our own times in the Church of elder Rome against Dioscorus? Although he had sinned in nothing against the faith, yet merely on account of ecclesiastical order he was anathematised after death by this same holy Roman Church. If, then, bishops who have sinned in nothing against the faith are subjected to anathema even after death merely on account of ecclesiastical order and for a financial cause, how much more Theodore, who sinned against God himself? As for the folly of those who say that those who died in their impiety ought not to be anathematised after death: [by that reasoning] neither ought Fathers who were unjustly condemned to be restored after death, as happened in the case of John of holy remembrance, bishop of the city of Constantinople, restored after death by the universal Church, and in that of Flavian of holy memory, he too bishop of the city of Constantinople, unjustly condemned in life but justly restored after death, both by Pope Leo of holy memory and by the holy synod of Chalcedon. From this it follows, according to their words, that heretics are numbered among the holy Fathers, as being freed from the condemnation due to them, while holy Fathers unjustly condemned are joined with heretics, as the unjust condemnation pronounced against them has not been annulled. But more than all must our Teacher, the Lord and our God Jesus Christ, be believed, who says of himself: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God" (John 3). And the Holy Spirit too says through the prophet David (Ps. 1) that the impious will not rise again in the judgement. Since, then, such a sentence has been pronounced by the Lord against every impious man, making no distinction between living and dead heretics, how do they dare to resist such a sentence and say that those who once acted impiously, and for this reason have already been condemned by the Lord, ought not to be condemned after death? And the divine Apostle too, who has Christ speaking in himself, pronounced such a sentence not only against men but even against angels, saying in the letter to the Galatians (ch. 1): "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel to you besides what we have preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel besides what you have received, let him be anathema." And who is so impious as to presume to say that the impious writings of Theodore, or any part of them, were ever handed down to the holy Church of God, and that whoever dared to say any such thing was not at once subjected to anathema by the holy Fathers?

If, then, after such a correct confession and condemnation of the heretics, while the pious understanding remains intact, anyone separates himself from the holy Church of God by contending over names or syllables or expressions, as though our piety lay not in realities but in names and expressions alone, such a man, as one who rejoices in dissensions, will render account for himself and for those deceived and to be deceived by him to our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ on the day of judgement. Amen.
Letter of the emperor Justinian to the holy synod concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and the rest.

It has always been the endeavour of the orthodox and pious emperors, our fathers, to cut off the heresies that arose from time to time through an assembly of the most religious priests, and, the right faith being sincerely preached, to keep the holy Church of God in peace. For this reason Constantine the Great too, when Arius was blaspheming and saying that the Son is not consubstantial with God the Father, but a creature, and made out of things that did not exist, assembled three hundred and eighteen Fathers at Nicaea, and, having himself been present at the council, after Arius had been condemned and anathematised, was eager to confirm the right faith, through which those divine Fathers confessed that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, and not a creature made out of things that did not exist, [and which] is sung to this very day. Theodosius the elder, when Macedonius was denying the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and Apollinarius his disciple was blaspheming the dispensation of the incarnate God the Word and saying that God the Word did not assume a human mind, but was united to flesh having a rational soul, assembled a hundred and fifty Fathers in the city of Constantinople, and, himself taking part in the council, when the aforesaid heretics had been condemned and struck with anathema together with their impious doctrines and followers, took care that the right faith should be preached. Theodosius the Younger, when the impious Nestorius was saying that God the Word is one and Christ another, and impiously introducing [the view] that the Word is by nature Son of God the Father, but Christ Son only by grace, and was denying that holy Mary is the Mother of God, assembled the first synod of Ephesus of two hundred holy Fathers, and, having sent officials who were to attend the council, ordered Nestorius himself also to be present and judgement to be passed on him; and after diligent examination they condemned and anathematised Nestorius together with his followers. When these things had followed thus, and the followers of the impious Nestorius had risen up against the most holy Cyril, they attempted (as far as lay in them) to rescind the sentence passed against Nestorius. But the emperor Theodosius, defending what had been so rightly judged against Nestorius and his impious doctrines, saw to it that the sentence of condemnation passed against him was held valid. Moreover, when they frivolously charged the divine Cyril before the emperor with certain other crimes as well, Cyril wrote to the emperor to this effect: "After it was reported to me, most pious emperor, that certain chatterers, like fierce wasps, were making your ears ring with their whisperings and belching out curses against me, idly asserting that I say the divine body of Christ was brought down from heaven and not taken from the holy Virgin, and likewise that I confess two sons according to the view of Nestorius, I thought I ought to say a few things against them to this effect: O fools, skilled in nothing except slander, how did you come to this view, and conceive such madness? For you certainly ought to have perceived clearly that almost our whole dispute about the faith arose from this, that we maintain that holy Mary is the Mother of God. Yet if, as they say, we say that the divine body of Christ came from heaven and was not born of her, how could she be called Mother of God?
